item.title: Most common players on eliminated teams from Week 3 in Yahoo Fantasy Death leagues — plus FAB waiver wire advice
item.description: Death Leagues have claimed more star players. Fantasy football analyst Scott Pianowski advises you on how to approach the waiver wire in Week 4.
item.content:encoded:
Every week I'll examine the most common NFL players on the teams eliminated in Yahoo Death Leagues, trying to figure out where the puck is headed. I will also offer some FAB advice ($1,000 cap is the Yahoo default), but please remember this area is highly context-sensitive and manager-specific.

Waiver strategy in Death Leagues

If you're new to this format, it's critical to understand that waiver strategy is significantly different in the world of Death Leagues.

You can often win a traditional fantasy league with modest help from the waiver wire, maybe a timely pickup or two. Sure, it's great if you crush the market and land the right guys — the best managers will always aim to be smart on the wire — but if your drafted team stays healthy and runs pure, some years that might be enough.

Immediate needs vs. playing the long game

In Death Leagues, the eventual winning manager will have assembled a MONSTER team at the end of the year, a juggernaut, a Pro Bowl-type of roster. And the way you build that beast is usually by having resources all season — not by using the majority of your FAB on a tantalizing early star. It's pivotal that you understand that the waiver wire should get stronger and stronger every week in Death leagues, because the eliminated manager is coming from a smaller and smaller league size every week.

Unless you have a draft touched by the fantasy angels, you are unlikely to win a Death League without a successful and careful waiver-wire strategy.

My Death League strategy is centered on the concept that I like my squad early in the year and I am confident I can beat at least one team per week while the field of opponents is large. Therefore, while I will dip my toes into the FAB market in the first quarter of the season, my primary goal is to keep major reserves in play for later in the year, when bye weeks hit and injuries are more prevalent — and the pool of opponents is smaller (so advancing is harder, in theory). Again, I urge you to remember: the waiver wire in Death Leagues gets stronger as the year gets deeper, a key reason to be judicious with your resources.

Not everyone will share my strategy, of course. If you want to chase major improvements and use the bulk of your FAB to load up quickly, then shoot your shot. Play the strategy you're comfortable with. Just understand that my recommendations are predicated on being careful early, and if you prefer something more aggressive, you'll have to jump the numbers up. You know your room better than an outsider does.

Understanding FAB recommendations

I will offer weekly FAB recommendations in three buckets:

Proactive: This means you highly covet this player, perhaps might even need this player. I realize these offers might not win if someone in your league is lighting money on fire, but as described above, that's often a short-sighted mistake in this format.

Reactive: This means you desire the player but the offer has to make sense for your short- or long-term strategy.

Keep Them Honest: This is an offer that is not designed to win, but might surprisingly land a player if your opponents are distracted by other talent available or unexpectedly passive that week. I often compare notes with other experienced Death League players and we're surprised at how often the Keep Them Honest offers actually win (this is also a portable strategy for regular season-long leagues; you never know when strange market behavior will come about).

One last note: understand that the FAB recommendations are with the assumption that you won't be making offers for every available player.

10 most common players on eliminated teams

WR Justin Jefferson, Vikings (22.1%)

In-game injuries are always going to be damaging to Death League players, though we can't be sure the Minnesota passing game will be reliable with QB Kyler Murray. Jefferson's MRI came back clean on his ankle, so he might be in play for Week 4. I'd like to wait for a bigger name in future weeks, but you have to consider your own roster and trust your instincts.

FAB Recommendation:

  • $220 proactive

  • $115 reactive

  • $55 keep them honest

RB De'Von Achane, Dolphins (21.7%)

He was looking like one of the busts of the season, tied to an offense that's got dozens of problems. Achane has an ACL tear and is done for the year, so don't forget to make modest FAB offers for Ollie Gordon II or Jaylen Wright.

WR Tetairoa McMillan, Panthers (21.1%)

Even with Xavier Legette scratched and Jalen Coker hurt in-game, McMillan failed to launch at Cleveland. It's hard to know how much of Carolina's fast start was matchup-boosted, but a bounce back against Detroit looks likely.

FAB Recommendation:

  • $150 proactive

  • $75 reactive

  • $20 keep them honest

RB Omarion Hampton, Chargers (16%)

The rushing lanes were hard to find in Buffalo, and Hampton was essentially ignored in the passing game. Worse yet, Keaton Mitchell was effective with a role increase, and the upcoming LAC schedule is a meat grinder. Very early in this Los Angeles season, it could be too late.

FAB Recommendation:

  • $125 proactive

  • $60 reactive

  • $20 keep them honest

RB Chase Brown, Bengals (15%)

His workload appears safe, though the Bengals haven't been able to unleash him as a receiver the last two weeks. Brown's good-not-elite talent level always made him more of a second-round pick, but he's still a slam-dunk starter in any traditional format.

FAB Recommendation:

  • $235 proactive

  • $150 reactive

  • $85 keep them honest

WR Jaylen Waddle, Broncos (14.8%)

He had his second washout game of the year, though at least Waddle managed a 2-point conversion to slightly mitigate the damage. Bo Nix doesn't look comfortable with new play caller Davis Webb, but hopefully a date with a slumping San Francisco defense will help the cause this week.

FAB Recommendation:

  • $160 proactive

  • $70 reactive

  • $20 keep them honest

QB Drake Maye, Patriots (14.3%)

We have to be reasonable given that he's working without top WR A.J. Brown, but Maye is also making bad decisions on a weekly basis. For the time being, he needs to be treated as a boom/bust QB2 as opposed to an every-week starter.

FAB Recommendation:

  • $70 proactive

  • $30 reactive

  • $5 keep them honest

RB TreVeyon Henderson, Patriots (13.3%)

He's going to share with Rhamondre Stevenson every week, and Henderson is seeing almost zero work in the passing game. The Patriots offense needs to be handled very carefully until further notice.

FAB Recommendation:

  • $65 proactive

  • $25 reactive

  • $4 keep them honest

WR Nico Collins, Texans (12.6%)

Injuries have been a part of his entire NFL career, and it's basically sunk the Houston offense this season. Collins has a shot to play in Week 4, and the upcoming schedule is decent. It all comes down to health.

FAB Recommendation:

  • $160 proactive

  • $75 reactive

  • $25 keep them honest

WR Amon-Ra St. Brown, Lions (12.6%)

The low yardage was a fluke, and even in a bad game, Brown still had a touchdown and eight targets. Detroit remains one of the most bankable carnivals in the NFL, so pay up.

FAB Recommendation:

  • $350 proactive

  • $200 reactive

  • $125 keep them honest

TE Dalton Kincaid, Bills (12.3%)

Variance bit at the wrong time, though at least he maintained a healthy snap share. The upcoming schedule isn't that friendly, but we like exposure to the Josh Allen passing game.

FAB Recommendation:

  • $125 proactive

  • $55 reactive

  • $12 keep them honest

item.title: Travis Hunter got a lot more work on the defensive side of the ball in Week 3
item.description: In Week 2, Jaguars cornerback/receiver Travis Hunter had only 31 defensive snaps.
item.content:encoded:
In Week 2, Jaguars cornerback/receiver Travis Hunter had only 31 defensive snaps. As expected, he got a lot more in Week 3.

Hunter was on the field for 45 defensive plays, in a game that featured his first career interception.

On offense, he continues to not do much. After getting six snaps in Week 2, he got only five in Week 3. He was targeted in neither game.

And so it seems as if the Jaguars are moving him toward being a full-time cornerback, and a very part-time receiver.

Whether that means he has accepted his apparent fate remains to be seen. He wants to play both sides of the ball. He wants to have the ball in his hands. And he seems to be concerned that, if he plays only defense and successfully locks down half of the field, he'll rarely touch the ball.

Regardless, his long-term best interests could be best served by playing only defense. Especially since the Jaguars have a great collection of receivers.

item.title: The 49ers’ injuries aren’t sustainable, but Brock Purdy might make them survivable
item.description: Purdy is playing at an MVP level, and is getting help from an oft-maligned area of the 49ers’ roster.
item.content:encoded:
The 49ers dodged several bullets with their injuries in their Week 3 win over the Arizona Cardinals.

Having lost defensive end Nick Bosa to a calf injury last week week — with the star pass rusher likely looking at around a month on the sideline — the 49ers saw several other key players go down in a 36-30 defeat of their division rivals on Sunday.

Mike Evans suffered a rib injury with two minutes left in the first half and was carted to the locker room, while the second half saw Trent Williams leave the game with a stinger and Dre Greenlaw sustain a quad injury.

Yet the saving grace for the 49ers is that, following evaluation, none of those injuries are serious. Evans is day-t0-day with a rib strain, Williams should be ready by Thursday while Greenlaw will be managed throughout the week with a quad contusion.

Still, there is an obvious sense of deja vu around the 49ers amid their excellent start to the season. The Niners are winning games despite a remarkable amount of injury adversity, just as they did in 2025.

Yet with 16 players already on injured reserve, and with the 49ers electing not to put Bosa on IR in part because of concern about having enough spots to designate players to return, it is clear San Francisco is close to a tipping point with injuries.

It is not sustainable for the 49ers to continue suffering injuries so consistently and keep winning. With tough games against the Denver Broncos and Seattle Seahawks on the horizon, fortunes for this injury-ravaged roster may soon change, and the harsh reality is that — even with this impressive start — it is difficult to envisage a roster in this shape seriously contending for the Super Bowl.

In this situation last season, the 49ers’ decimated roster unsurprisingly hit a ceiling, and the result was 41-6 divisional round loss to the Seahawks that ended an admirable campaign.

Still, for as much as the sheer scale of the injuries has presented significant challenges for San Francisco, outside of Ricky Pearsall, the 49ers have yet to lose a member their roster who could be considered a blue-chip player for the season.

That is a crucial difference from 2025, when the 49ers lost Bosa and Fred Warner for the season within the first six weeks and also had to deal with a multi-week injury to quarterback Brock Purdy.

And, though their current form amid the injuries doesn’t seem sustainable, the 49ers have hope that it can continue because of the play that is being sustained by two critical components of the offense.

Purdy provides hope amid yet more adversity

That Purdy’s performance against the Cardinals was arguably his worst of the season so far speaks to how well he is playing.

Arizona succeeded in making life a lot more difficult for Purdy than either the Los Angeles Rams or Miami Dolphins did, and there were periods of the game in which the offense sputtered.

Purdy did not put up the spectacular completion percentage numbers that defined the first two weeks, but the final stat line still made for very impressive reading.

He completed only 55.6 percent of his passes against the Cardinals, but still threw for 297 yards and four touchdowns.

Through three games, Purdy boasts a completion percentage of 72.3, has 789 passing yards and leads the NFL with nine touchdown passes while throwing just one interception.

Purdy is also first in the NFL in success rate on passing plays (63.9%) and adjusted yards per attempt and adjusted net yards per attempt (both 11.1). He leads the NFL in passer rating (133.1) and QBR (93.8).

In terms of Expected Points Added, Purdy’s EPA per play of 0.59 over the first three weeks ranks first of any quarterback since 2016, per Sumer Sports.

Put simply, Purdy is playing at an MVP level right now, with his standard exemplified by three standout plays in Week 3. His 23-yard touchdown pass to Mike Evans was a superb demonstration of the accuracy that has played a substantial role in his high completion percentage, while the sequence that effectively ended the game as a contest was an encapsulation of the upside he possesses as an athlete.

Purdy was robbed of an early MVP moment when he saw a 35-yard scramble for a touchdown brought back because of what looked a harsh holding penalty against George Kittle. Two plays later, though, Purdy rolled out after a play-fake and found a wide-open Kittle for a 20-yard score to end Arizona’s comeback effort.

Asked if any quarterback is playing better than Purdy right now, Kyle Shanahan told his post-game press conference: “I’d be surprised, but I don’t study the other quarterbacks right now, so I don’t really know what anyone else is doing except for the guys that we go against.

“I don’t get to see any of that, but I think it’s really hard to play much better than he’s playing right now.”

All the numbers indicate you cannot play any better than Purdy is doing right now, but he is being supported by an offensive line that is doing an excellent job through three weeks.

Indeed, despite concerns about the makeup on the interior O-Line and the injury to Williams on Sunday, the 49ers have still yet to give up a sack.

Per Pro Football Reference, the 49ers have allowed a pressure rate of just 13.5%, the best in the NFL. Pressures and sacks are a quarterback and offensive line stat, and those hugely impressive numbers reflect a quarterback with an elite understanding of how to move in the pocket and an oft-maligned O-Line making huge strides.

The challenge for both Purdy and the O-Line is maintaining that kind of form as the difficulty level ramps up.

Of course, there are going to be some down weeks for Purdy and the offensive line is obviously not going to go the entire season without giving up a sack. But the level of play at the quarterback position and in the trenches are primary reasons for hope for the 49ers that this year could be different, and that the injuries don’t necessarily have to limit what they can achieve.

The defenses of both Denver and Seattle will severely test the 49ers up front and provide challenges to Purdy that he has yet to face through weeks.

If Purdy and the O-Line can rise to these forthcoming challenges and perform at somewhere close to the standard they have each produced so far, then that would provide cause for expectations to rise significantly.

San Francisco can’t afford for the injuries to keep piling up, and the 49ers desperately need Bosa back as soon as possible. But Purdy and those protecting him have to this point served as key differentiators from last season. As long as that remains the case, the 49ers have a chance of surviving their adversity and mounting a more serious challenge than their 2025 injuries allowed.

item.title: Cowboys injury updates: Jonathan Bullard, Jalen Thompson to miss time
item.description: The Cowboys are pretty banged up on defense
item.content:encoded:
The Dallas Cowboys are ailing on defense.

It was reported on Monday that safety Jalen Thompson, one of the handful of players banged up in last week’s loss in Brazil, would miss a month or more, and Jerry Jones corroborated that on Tuesday morning during his appearance on 105.3 The Fan.

Jerry also noted that Jonathan Bullard is likely to miss around 3-4 weeks and that Shavon Revel has an injury situation going on as well, but they are optimistic there.

It goes without saying that the Cowboys are down significantly on that side of the ball. P.J. Locke and Malik Hooker are players who were hurt on defense even before the game, so the team is going to have to get a bit creative.

Complicating matters even more is that the Cowboys have two games between now and next Thursday night. There truly is no rest for the weary.

item.title: Chargers Power Rankings Roundup: Bolts’ downward slide continues at 0-3
item.description: The Chargers continue to tumble down this week’s NFL power rankings after dropping to 0-3.
item.content:encoded:
The Chargers were as close as they have been all year to earning their first win this past Sunday. Five takeaways by the defense usually means victory is assured. Yet somehow, that wasn’t the case by the time the clock hit zero at Highmark Stadium.

When it was all said and done, the Chargers held a +4 advantage in the turnover battle while still leaving on the wrong end of a 24-16 result. The offense scored just 10 points off those five turnovers which was nowhere near enough cushion to hold off the Bills by the time they got their act together.

Understandably so, that debacle has led to the Chargers dropping even further down this week’s NFL power rankings.

Let’s check out how bad the damage is.

CBS Sports – #24

“They played in desperation mode on the road against the Bills, and it still wasn’t good enough. The schedule is brutal, and a 0-9 start is possible.” – Pete Prisco

Sports Illustrated – #27

“Column on the Chargers, who should be investigated for wire fraud.” – Conor Orr

ESPN – #27

“Expectations were high for the 2025 first-round pick, given how running backs have thrived with OC Mike McDaniel at other stops. But Hampton has been a disappointment so far. He was the 12th running back in ADP, but his 31 points ranks 22nd. Hampton also saw a decreased workload in Week 3 after struggles in his first two weeks. As the Chargers move forward, this could become more of a split backfield with Hampton and Keaton Mitchell, who averaged 6.5 yards per carry to Hampton’s 3.7 in Buffalo.” — Kris Rhim

Sporting News – #29

‘‘The Chargers were more active defensively to turn over the Bills multiple times. But Jim Harbaugh saw more awful offense with Justin Herbert failing to stop his own giveaway woes. They, like the Texans, are straight-up bad at this point.” – Vinnie Iyer

Pro Football Talk – #29

“Justin Herbert has replaced Joe Burrow as the ‘veteran QB most likely to change teams in 2027.”’ – Mike Florio

USA Today – #29

“The last time they were 0-3 was 2017, when Philip Rivers was the quarterback, and the team was playing in a suburban L.A. soccer stadium. The more things change …” – Nate Davis

Bleacher Report – #29

“The Los Angeles Chargers are completely lost. An 0-3 start has them swimming for a life raft with one unlikely to appear since the Seattle Seahawks, Denver Broncos and Kansas City Chiefs are next on the docket.” 

“Surprisingly, the Chargers’ biggest disconnect can be found on offense, where quarterback Justin Herbert isn’t executing Mike McDaniel’s offensive scheme.”

“This past offseason, McDaniel’s hire was viewed as one of the league’s best, because he brought a proven track record as a play-caller. Instead, the Chargers are in disarray, Herbert is playing poorly and the unit ranks among the league’s bottom-feeders in total offense.” — Brent Sobleski 

The Athletic – #29

“This was supposed to be Justin Herbert’s year. (Or was that last year? It’s hard to keep up.) The Chargers’ two heralded tackles aren’t playing great, and they’re having to start a rookie at center, but this is Year 7 for Herbert, who has more interceptions than touchdowns (4-to-3) and the third-worst passer rating in the league (73.4). Offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel was supposed to fix this, but it hasn’t happened yet, and the Seahawks, Broncos, Chiefs and Rams are next.” – Chad Graff and Josh Kendall

item.title: NFL Power Rankings Week 4 Roundup: Chiefs’ hot start has them near top
item.description: Let’s see where Kansas City is ranked for Week 4 of the NFL season.
item.content:encoded:
The 2026 NFL regular season’s Week 3 featured the Kansas City Chiefs beating the Miami Dolphins, moving to 3-0, one of five NFL teams with that record.

Let’s see how the national media responds in this week’s sampling of power rankings:

NFL.com: 2

(Up from 4)

The Chiefs are very aware of who they are just three weeks into the season. They didn’t need to fully exert themselves on Sunday, earning a professional win against a scrappy but undermanned Dolphins team. They decreased Kenneth Walker III’s touches, too, which was a requirement for me in such a matchup, especially with most of the season still ahead.

ESPN: 3

(Up from 4)

Fantasy surprise: RB Kenneth Walker III

Most fantasy owners knew Walker was a good choice, especially after his impressive postseason run to help the Seahawks win the Super Bowl. But not even the Chiefs could have expected this level of production from Walker, who has the second-most total fantasy points at RB this season. He has already produced 442 scrimmage yards and four total touchdowns. Walker is the first player in franchise history to have two games with a rushing and receiving touchdown within the first three weeks, per ESPN Research. — Nate Taylor

The Athletic: 3

(Up from 4)

QB confidence: All the way back

Patrick Mahomes is tied for second in the NFL in passing touchdowns (seven) and looks as scary as ever now that he’s sharing a backfield with Kenneth Walker III. Walker leads the league in rushing (360 yards), and Mahomes is using play action at a higher rate (32.1 percent) than he ever has. Mahomes was 20-of-24 for 246 yards Sunday to hold off the surprisingly plucky Miami Dolphins.

— Chad Graff and Josh Kendall

Pro Football Talk: 2

(Up from 4)

The Chiefs are back . . . to playing with their food before winning easily.

— Mike Florio

CBSSports.com: 3

(Up from 5)

At 3-0, the people who buried them need to admit they were wrong. They play a big one this week at Las Vegas against the unbeaten Raiders.

— Pete Prisco

Yahoo! Sports: 4

(Up from 6)

The Chiefs are 3-0 but if there’s a concern, it’s still the passing offense around Patrick Mahomes. In particular, Xavier Worthy has been surprisingly quiet. In three games, he has 18, 25 and 20 yards. Miami has a poor secondary and Worthy managed only two catches for 20 yards. The hope that the 2024 first-round draft pick could break out in his third season is dwindling.

Other than that, the Chiefs are doing well. The worry is what happens if Kenneth Walker, who is carrying the offense, wears down under the biggest workload of his career or misses time. There’s not much else around him for Mahomes to work with.

— Frank Schwab

USA Today: 2

(Up from 5)

RB Kenneth Walker III is averaging a league-best 120 rushing yards per game while continuing to give every indication he’s unlocked the AFC’s top-ranked offense anew. Next, a battle for first place in the AFC West at Las Vegas, where QB Patrick Mahomes is 6-0.

— Nate Davis

Sports Illustrated: 2

(Up from 3)

Here is a bit of a mea culpa and explainer on why the Kansas City Chiefs are very real. I’d check it out if I were you.

— Conor Orr

FOX Sports: 4

(Up from 8)

Everyone was finally convinced they were back to their old, dynastic selves, and then they go and let a terrible Dolphins team hang around for an awfully long time. But they are 3-0 and not every game can be perfect, I guess. They’re on the rise, though. They have a whole new dimension with RB Kenneth Walker III, and they still have the ever-dangerous Patrick Mahomes and an array of weapons. 

Kansas City also has a pretty soft schedule. With the Raiders up next, they’re looking at 4-0 heading into their bye. So I have a feeling this isn’t the last stop on their climb up the charts.

Stat To Know: With the Chiefs win on Sunday, Patrick Mahomes passed Tom Brady for the third-most wins by a player in his first 10 seasons since 1950. 

— Ralph Vacchiano

item.title: Fantasy football Start ‘Em, Sit ‘Em: 16 players to start or sit in Week 4
item.description: A plethora of running back injuries will have fantasy football managers looking to stream at the position. Here's who to start and sit in Week 4.
item.content:encoded:
Injury hits just keep on coming for fantasy football managers during the 2026 NFL season.

In Week 2, several prominent quarterbacks went down with significant injuries, including one that knocked New York Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart out for the season. Week 3 saw several prominent running backs get hurt, with De'Von Achane suffering a season-ending ACL tear while Breece Hall and Travis Etienne Jr. are also battling maladies that could sideline them.

That will force fantasy football managers to rely on their depth as they look to make difficult start 'em, sit 'em decisions in Week 4.

The good news? With three weeks of data under their belts, fantasy managers will have a better idea of which matchups are the best for streaming options.

Who can you start and sit in fantasy football for Week 4 of the 2026 NFL season? USA TODAY Sports outlines eight players to start and eight to sit:

Fantasy football players to start in Week 4

Quarterbacks

  • Kyler Murray, Minnesota Vikings (vs. Miami Dolphins)

Murray is still getting his feet wet with the Vikings, but he gets a favorable matchup in Week 4. The Dolphins have allowed an average of 231 passing yards per game and eight total touchdowns to the position. Kevin O'Connell may view this as an opportunity to work out the kinks in Minnesota's Murray-led passing attack, which could lead the 29-year-old to have his first multi-touchdown day of the season.

  • Marcus Mariota, Washington Commanders (vs. Indianapolis Colts)

There's a non-zero chance Jayden Daniels (elbow) is able to suit up for Week 4. However, if he can't, Mariota will be a great play against a Colts team allowing the fifth-most fantasy points per game (FPPG) to quarterbacks. Mariota just threw for 183 yards and three touchdowns against a loaded Seahawks defense, so he should be well positioned to expose a weaker Indianapolis stop unit.

Running backs

  • Braelon Allen, New York Jets (at Chicago Bears)

Breece Hall is dealing with a thigh injury so his status for Week 4 is murky. If Hall misses time, Allen would slot into New York's lead-back role and would get a chance to face a Bears defense allowing 117 rushing yards per game. That, plus Allen's likely role as a goal-line hammer, will give him RB2 upside.

  • J.K. Dobbins, Denver Broncos (at San Francisco 49ers)

Dobbins is averaging just 3.5 yards per carry but is facing a 49ers defense dealing with countless injuries to its defensive line. The 49ers just allowed Jeremiyah Love to rack up 109 scrimmage yards and a touchdown against them, so Dobbins could be in line for a solid day if he continues to get a high-volume of touches in Denver's offense.

Wide receivers

  • Jordan Addison, Minnesota Vikings (vs. Miami Dolphins)

Justin Jefferson is dealing with an ankle injury and may not play in Week 4 because of it. That will open the door for Addison to serve as Minnesota's No. 1 receiver in a favorable matchup with the Dolphins. Fire him up as a clear-cut WR2 who could emerge as a top-15 play this week.

  • Keenan Allen, Indianapolis Colts (vs. Washington Commanders)

Allen established himself as the Colts' clear-cut No. 2 receiver with Alec Pierce out of the lineup by catching 6 of 9 targets against the Texans for 63 yards and a touchdown. Next up for the 34-year-old will be a Week 4 date with a Commanders defense that has allowed the most FPPG to receivers this season. Allen should emerge as a quality flex play in that matchup.

Tight end

  • Kyle Pitts, Atlanta Falcons (at New Orleans Saints)

This is Pitts' last stand, at least for fantasy purposes. He only has two catches for 20 yards across his first three games but he should do better against a Saints defense that has allowed 25 receptions to tight ends this season, second-most in the league. If he can't deliver in this matchup, it will be safe to drop him, in all likelihood.

Defense/special teams

  • Seattle Seahawks (vs. Los Angeles Chargers)

Don't be scared off by the Seahawks' lackluster showing against Mariota and the Commanders. Mike Macdonald's stop unit is still strong and is in a favorable matchup against a struggling Chargers offense. Justin Herbert has been sacked multiple times in all three games this season and has tossed at least one interception each time out, giving Seattle's defense a high floor playing at home.

Fantasy football players to sit in Week 4

Quarterbacks

  • Kirk Cousins, Las Vegas Raiders (vs. Kansas City Chiefs)

Cousins has thrown three touchdowns in each of his first three games with the Raiders. Fantasy managers hoping to see him post similar production against the Chiefs may be disappointed, as Kansas City has allowed the fewest FPPG to opposing quarterbacks this season, and just two total passing touchdowns across three games.

  • Jared Goff, Detroit Lions (at Carolina Panthers)

The Lions have an explosive, high-scoring offense, but their matchup with the Panthers looks more favorable for Jahmyr Gibbs than it does Goff. The Panthers are allowing just 172.3 passing yards per game, sixth-fewest in the NFL, while their 193.3 rushing yards per game surrendered ranks dead-last. Goff could still post low-end QB1 numbers, but his upside is capped.

Running backs

  • Ollie Gordon II, Miami Dolphins (at Minnesota Vikings)

Gordon may be in line to take a lion's share of the Dolphins' running back snaps after Achane's season-ending ACL tear, but his matchup against the Vikings is a tough one. Brian Flores' blitz-happy defense has allowed the fourth-fewest FPPG to running backs this season and just 3.5 yards per carry, which should give it a unit a chance to significantly slow a shaky Dolphins offense.

  • Alvin Kamara, New Orleans Saints (vs. Atlanta Falcons)

Kamara may see a larger role as Travis Etienne deals with a hamstring injury, but the veteran is facing a Falcons defense that has allowed the fewest FPPG to running backs this season. Kamara will also be splitting touches with Kendre Miller and, potentially, CJ Donaldson on the goal line, so it's best to see how New Orleans' rotation looks before blindly putting faith in Kamara to produce.

Wide receivers

  • Emeka Egbuka, Tampa Bay Buccaneers (vs. Green Bay Packers)

Egbuka has been a steady fantasy contributor this season, but he hasn't emerged as the top-tier weapon many who selected him early were hoping. Now, he will be tasked with remaining productive as undrafted rookie Jalon Daniels draws into the lineup to replace Baker Mayfield. Daniels could perform well, but it's probably better to wait and see what he can do before starting Egbuka.

  • Jameson Williams, Detroit Lions (at Carolina Panthers)

Williams hasn't yet logged more than four catches or 49 yards in a game this season. That seems unlikely to change against a Panthers team that is allowing the second-fewest FPPG to receivers, especially since Carolina's defense will incentivize a run-heavy game plan for Detroit.

Tight end

  • Mark Andrews, Baltimore Ravens (vs. Tennessee Titans)

Andrews has been reasonably productive to start the season, but he hasn't yet found the end-zone. That seems unlikely to change against a Titans defense that has surrendered just 48 yards and no touchdowns to tight ends thus far in 2026.

Defense/special teams

  • Houston Texans (vs. Dallas Cowboys)

The Texans haven't yet lived up to the hype defensively, as they are surrendering a middle-of-the-pack 25 points per game this season while creating just three takeaways. Houston's sack floor is solid, but in what could be a shootout against a great Dallas offense, it's hard to recommend trusting the Texans as an upper-echelon play.

item.title: Snap Reactions, Week 3: What playing time says about Seahawks depth chart at skill positions
item.description: As Seattle looks to rebound in Week 4, a look at the snap counts from the loss to the Commanders provides some interesting insight to the current depth chart.
item.content:encoded:
The defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks went on the road in Week 3, facing off against the Washington Commanders, losing for the first time since Week 12 of the 2025 season.

While the final score was close, between an ineffective running game and three turnovers that led to 21 points for the commanders, it’s a game the Seahawks will look back on and feel they should have won.

On the offensive side of things, Seattle had a solid day outside of turnovers. The run game certainly was not where the team or fans would like it to be, but Sam Darnold showed once again that he is capable of leading an offense even when the run game isn’t working.

The offensive snap counts are very interesting for several reasons. Likely the most talked about snap counts on the offensive side of the ball is at right guard, where there was a clean 60/40 split for snaps between Christian Haynes and Beau Stephens.

Perhaps more interesting, though, is what the snap counts say about other position groups. Tight end is unquestionably A.J. Barner and then a huge gap before either of Eric Saubert or Elijah Arroyo, both of whom finished with 18 offensive snaps. At receiver All-Universe Jaxon Smith-Njigba is the unquestioned leader of the group, with Cooper Kupp and Rashid Shaheed seeing similar snap counts to the 2025 season. Tory Horton wouldn’t be expected to see a huge amount of work as he continues working his way back into things, but it bears watching whether he earns more snaps in the coming weeks.

Another position that bears watching is running back, where former undrafted free agent George Holani and former undrafted free agent Emmanuel Wilson both outsnapped 2026 first round pick Jadarian Price. Similar to Horton, Price wouldn’t necessarily be expected to have a huge workload after leaving the Week 2 win over the Arizona Cardinals due to injury, so at least at this point being outsnapped by more veteran players is likely less of a concern than ball security.

On the defensive side of the ball, there weren’t a whole lot of surprises. Nick Emmanwori played 36 defensive snaps in his second game back on the field following surgery in the offseason, while Nehemiah Pritchett played just over half of the defensive snaps in the game. That is noteworthy for Pritchett in that it marks the third time in three games that he has played more than fifty percent of defensive snaps, something he had only done twice in his career prior to this season.

And when it comes to special teams, just as it has been in recent seasons, it’s Brady Russell’s world and everyone else just lives in it. Russell led the Seahawks with 28 special teams snaps, while Mike Morris was second at 24 in his first regular season action of the year. Tyrice Knight, Patrick O’Connell and Chazz Surratt all logged 23 special teams snaps to round out the top five for the team.

And now it’s on to a second consecutive matchup against a winless opponent, as the Los Angeles Chargers bring their 0-3 record to Lumen Sunday afternoon in search of their first win of the season.

item.title: Ben Johnson: Case Keenum's touchdown run was a "Mike Martz special" play call
item.description: Bears head coach Ben Johnson has earned a reputation as an offensive innovator, but he didn't come up with the idea that led to one of his team's touchdowns in Monday's 27-7 win over the Eagles.
item.content:encoded:
Bears head coach Ben Johnson has earned a reputation as an offensive innovator, but he didn't come up with the idea that led to one of his team's touchdowns in Monday's 27-7 win over the Eagles.

Quarterback Case Keenum ran for a one-yard score in the fourth quarter on a play that saw the two Chicago guards pull in opposite directions while Keenum followed center Garrett Bradbury up the middle for the score. After the game, Johnson credited former Rams head coach Mike Martz with coming up with the play design.

“That’s a Mike Martz special right there, that's the old sucker sneak," Johnson said. "I think they were a little bit tight initially and then they stemmed out at the last second, which gave us the green light to get to that play. It’s an old play, an old but a good play right there.”

Martz memorably called the play during Super Bowl XXXVI and it resulted in a Kurt Warner touchdown run. Johnson was a teenager when that game was played, but Martz's ingenuity stuck with him.

item.title: Patriots injury analysis: The hits keep coming
item.description: Analyzing the Patriots’ injury situation after their Week 3 loss.
item.content:encoded:
The New England Patriots’ third game of the 2026 season was an abject disaster. The offense was all sort out of sync, the defense played its worst football in two years, and special teams didn’t make many positive contributions either.

To make matters worse, the team sustained multiple injuries. While not quite as dramatic as the Week 2 win over Pittsburgh, the 35-6 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars was still a bad one from a health perspective. For a 1-2 team already reeling, the hits just keep coming.

Patriots injury analysis: NFL Week 3

RT Morgan Moses: The veteran right tackle was a limited participant in practice all week but eventually made the trip to Jacksonville without a game designation. That said, he did not look his best on the field from the first drive on. Moses hobbled on several occasions and was pulled from the game for rookie Caleb Lomu in the late third quarter.

CB Christian Gonzalez: The Patriots’ best player had his shoulder checked out after a physical third-down tackle in the first quarter. No injury was announced by the team and no time missed by Gonzalez.

C Jared Wilson: Wilson played all 51 snaps alongside quarterback Drake Maye, and he did so despite suffering a cut on his right middle finger early in the game — the second time an injury like that happened this season after Week 1 versus Seattle. According to Maye, the bleeding might have contributed to his fumble in the first quarter.

DT Christian Barmore: Barmore was announced as questionable to return early in the second quarter and did leave for the locker room due to a shoulder issue. He did return to the sideline shortly thereafter and reentered the game later during that period without showing any obvious limitations.

RG Greg Van Roten: Already starting in place of an injured Mike Onwenu, the Patriots’ right guard was slow to get up after a third-down play in the second quarter. He headed into the blue medical tent to have his thigh checked out and was announced as questionable to return. He never did, with third-stringer Walter Rouse finishing the contest in Van Roten’s place.

CB Carlton Davis III: Making his comeback after missing the previous game with a neck injury, Davis remained down on one knee after a sideline tackle in the third quarter. He was checked out by the training staff, but walked off under his own power and into the medical tent. He eventually returned on the next series after missing a total of five defensive plays.

LT Will Campbell: One of the few Patriots to perform at an adequate level on Sunday, Campbell was slow to get up after a short run in the late fourth quarter. He limped back to the huddle, stayed in the game, and finished with a 100% playing time share and no injury ever being announced.

OL Ben Brown: One play after Campbell, Ben Brown showed some discomfort following a short catch-and-run. The backup center also remained in the contest and showed no obvious limitations before the final whistle.

What this means for the Patriots

If we look at the Jaguars game and the Patriots’ injury situation coming out of it from a “glass half full” perspective, we can say that only one player — Greg Van Roten — was truly unable to finish the contest. The others suffered some bumps and bruises, but seemingly nothing that should be considered a long-term concern.

However, where there is a glass half full, there also is a glass half empty. And if we use that point of view, we see a Patriots team that a) saw even more players get banged up, and b) is now down to its third-string right guard.

After Mike Onwenu was lost to a fractured ankle in Week 2, Week 3 saw his replacement leave before the half only to be replaced by a late-August trade pickup who had played zero regular season snaps at the position since entering the NFL in 2024. Walter Rouse very well might turn into a serviceable player at some point, but the progression from Onwenu, to Van Roten, to him is still one downgrade after the other.

Maybe Van Roten will be able to get back in time for the upcoming game against the Buffalo Bills. Even so, the right guard spot — and the right side of the O-line in general given Morgan Moses’ own issues — is a problem right now.

The first indication of may or may not be available for Week 4 will come on Wednesday, first at practice and then via the injury report. The Patriots will visit the 3-0 Bills on Sunday for a 1 p.m. ET kickoff.

item.title: Rookies Mike Washington, Zeke Masses come up big in Week 3 win
item.description: How did Las Vegas’ rookie class fare in Week 3?
item.content:encoded:
Here is a look at how the Las Vegas Raiders’ 2026 draft class (eight of the 10 picks are on the 53-man roster) fared in a 35-27 Week 3 win at the New Orleans Saints and what to look for Sunday at home against the Kansas City Chiefs:

Fernando Mendoza:
The No. 1 overall pick served as Kirk Cousins backup. He did not play. But he’s on a streak. Mendoza hasn’t been part of a team that has lost since 2024.

Treydan Stukes:

The Raiders’ second-round pick was out because of a concussion he suffered in Week 2. He is expected to be back this week and the Raiders need him against Travis Kelce.

Trey Zuhn:

The third-round pick played five offensive plays after playing two plays in Week 2. He was even lined up in an H-back role Sunday. Coach Klint Kubiak is finding ways to get his players involved.

Jermod McCoy:

The fourth-round pick played 12 special teams snaps, but none on defense. He played 18 defensive snaps in Week 2.

Mike Washington:

The fourth-round pick played 16 percent of the snaps after playing 19 percent of the snaps in the first two games. Washington made his snaps count as he had a 36-yard touchdown run in the third quarter to get the Raiders back in the game as they finished the game with 19 unanswered points. He has 102 rushing yards on 15 carries.

Dalton Johnson:

The fifth-round pick safety was a healthy scratch for the third straight game. Him being inactive with Stukes out isn’t a great sign.

Zeke Masses:

The fifth-round pick is now a clear starting cornerback. He started for an injured Darien Porter in Week 2. Porter was healthy in Week 3 and Masses still started. Masses made a big interception in the fourth quarter at the Saints and he has three interceptions in the past two games. He’s an exciting playmaker.

Malik Benson:

The sixth-round pick played four offensive snaps and two on special teams. He was targeted once with no catches and had one punt return for 13 yards.

item.title: Broncos vs. Rams: The No Bull Review
item.description: No Bull thoughts, opinions, and analysis on the Denver Broncos defeat of the Los Angeles Rams 30 - 26 Sunday Night
item.content:encoded:
Don’t you dare count out this Denver Broncos team after one bad half of football. This is still the same Denver Broncos we cheered for last year. This team never stops fighting. The opponent may be absolutely kicking the Broncos up and down the field on both sides of the ball for 2 quarters. Sorry, Rams. NFL games are 4 quarters long, and these Denver Broncos live and breathe it.

Especially in the rarefied air of their home field in front of the sold-out throng of Broncos Country.

Sean Payton is still the head coach of this team. He has Davis Webb, Vance Joseph, and his players ready to do their jobs on game day.

I’m not going to sit here and say this team doesn’t have flaws. We’re going to talk about them. I’m going to point out the same weaknesses we’ve been talking about on this team for at least a year, if not two.

But I’m going to give praise where it is due and shout from the rooftops that this team is packed with winners. These guys believe in each other and their coaches. The coaches know how to make adjustments and help their players when things aren’t going to plan.

Underestimate this Broncos team at your own peril, NFL. 

Offense

This game was very Jekyll and Hyde from one half of the game to the other. The big problem with the first half is the same problem with these Denver Broncos over the past year when Sean Payton was calling plays. Davis Webb is starting darn near every drive early with a run. He’s then calling simple short passing plays mostly at or behind the line of scrimmage or within 5 yards of it.

This is predictable, and teams have been largely burying the Broncos early in games because of how predictable the play calling is. The big problem is the pass game design and how they execute the plays early in games.


For whatever reason, Bo Nix isn’t throwing downfield much at all early in games. That’s the one thing that Payton and Davis Webb need to change soon. This team is capable of putting teams away early; they just need to play football in the first half the way they do in the 2nd half, with more throws downfield in the play designs being executed by the offense.

I think it is worth noting that this problem can be play call and design, or it can be player execution. It is largely impossible for us as fans to understand, looking from the outside. We do not know what the call is, what options exist for the quarterback to execute, and what reads are being made that dictate where the ball needs to go. I’m just saying that whatever the cause, this offense is limited by this very obvious trend early in games that we’ve seen both this season and last season.

When the 2nd half came around (starting with our 2nd drive in the 3rd quarter), the team finally started leaning on the run game. I’ll point out that the running game wasn’t even terribly successful. That part doesn’t matter. The team often got to 2nd and 7ish, then 3rd and 4 or 5. These are much more manageable downs than 3rd and 7 or more. Webb needs to be braver about running the rock more often early in the games. This should not constantly be a 2nd-half adjustment to play calling.

Quarterbacks

Bo Nix absolutely has ice water running in his veins. He thrives on being backed into a corner with the odds stacked against him. It can be maddening to watch him derp through half of a football game only to turn into Superman in the 2nd half, but those of us in Broncos Country that have been watching since the 80s or before are kinda used to this brand of football. We’ve got some critiques of Nix to talk about, but the baseline is that I love this player and what he brings to this football team. There is no quarterback in the NFL today I would rather have on my team than Nix, full stop.

So let’s not forget that Nix is a young NFL quarterback. He’s showing it with some of his choices where he’s locking onto one route and throwing it regardless of what is in front of his eyes. He should have had two more interceptions in this game from throws that should have just gone into the stands. Hopefully he’s getting coached to know his limits (the end zone bomb attempt to Sutton that came up far short when he was throwing off his back foot moving to his right) and read defensive leverage and know when your guy is owned (he had another one of these poor throws tonight that was dropped). The interesting thing is that his one recorded interception in this game was from being hit, not necessarily making a bad throw. 

Back to the positives: His 2-point conversion to Waddle was an absolutely filthy, undefendable dime. You can not throw a pass more perfectly on and out and up to the back of the end zone than what he did there.

His touchdown to Bryant was also smartly placed high so that his receiver could high point it and shield it from being batted down.

Line

Quinn Meinerz absolutely embarrassed Aaron Donald by getting him going sideways, lifting him off the ground, and throwing him down for a pancake block. Meinerz is an All-Pro guard still. Interestingly, after this, Donald didn’t line up much across from Meinerz. Also, suspiciously, Meinerz got texted about being drug tested following the game.

McGlinchey costs us our first drive, getting worked into Nix’s lap. To his credit, he was a key blocker who got pulled out to the flat to help Bo get us down to 1st and goal at the ½ yard line. He played that to perfection and did a great job blocking for Bo.

Running Backs

RJ Harvey may not have done much in the run game (2 runs for 6 yards), but his catches out of the backfield were money. He led all receivers with 6 catches for 41 yards. His play as a joker even set up the big pass to Bryant later in the game, where a defensive back crashed down to stop Harvey, leaving Bryant wide open with no defenders in 20 yards.

JK Dobbins was a dependable runner for the Broncos this game. He had 17 rushes for a paltry 49 yards, but he kept the offense in manageable situations. He did get lucky on his fumble with the ball bouncing directly into Bryant’s hands. He looks like a dinged-up player to me (which he likely is with a sore hammy). I’d still like to see more than a 6-yard gain as his best out of 17 attempts.

Tyler Badie needs some love for all the work he’s doing for this team. Sure, he only ran once for 2 yards. But he had a superb route out of the backfield for a 10+ play on 2nd and 10. More importantly, he was in on many of our obvious passing situations as a pass blocker.

Receivers

Pat Bryant absolutely slayed and honestly should get more targets. His touchdown catch was not an easy catch to make, and he went up and got the score. He also absolutely bailed the team out of a 2nd and 20 with a crossing route wide open for a huge gain. He also had his defender beat on an out route on the final drive, got bumped to draw a pass interference flag late in the game. And for the record, yes, that was pass interference. Section 5 of the officiating handbook, article 2: 

“Initiating contact with an opponent by shoving or pushing off, thus creating separation.”

The defender shoved Bryant in the back, which is what the flag was for. When you slow-mo the end of the play, it looks like no big deal. The problem is that most of the Los Angeles Rams fans and other ass hats in the media (including Collinsworth and their hack ref from the announcing crew for Sunday Night Football) aren’t looking at the whole play. They are cherry-picking the end in slow-mo instead of watching the whole play.

Cortland Sutton had a pretty up-and-down game. He only hauled in 3 of his 7 targets for 46 yards. But man, were two of those catches important. He made our first first down out of sheer grit. He ran a go on the sideline, got interfered with, and still fought through to make the catch. It was a savage play that gained us 27 much-needed yards late. Also, credit to Sutton for saving Bo from a yolo pick. He leapt up and defended that ball by knocking it out of the defender’s grasp.

Jaylen Waddle outside of the 2-point conversion had a pretty rough game as well. We were really forcing it to him by and large. He had a drop and just didn’t connect as well in this game, catching 2 of 7 targets for 10 yards.

Nate Adkins runs really sneaky good routes out of blocking formations, which makes him a deadly outlet receiver in goal-line situations. This is the 2nd game in a row where he’s caught a walk-in touchdown as an outlet receiver to the sideline.

Defense

Vance Joseph is masterful at sorting out what opponents are doing and adjusting his defense as the game wears on. The adjustments he made at halftime (and let’s be absolutely clear: he very much did, regardless of the nonsense Bo was spouting about how they just stuck to their game plan at halftime) were masterful. He dialed up timely blitzes and creative stunts to push the pocket and make Stafford uncomfortable.

They did a lot of bending but not breaking early in the game. They played a lot of press man, and the Rams largely tore it to shreds. This defense plays as good as any defense in the NFL once it gets into the red zone, though. Holding the Rams to just 16 points in 4 drives into the red zone was excellent.

Front 7

Zach Allen does not get enough credit for just how frigging good his game is. He is the most disruptive defensive lineman in the NFL. He had a timely sack late in the 3rd quarter, had a tackle for loss, and count them: 5 quarterback hits. He’s one of the NFL’s best gap-breaking linemen and impacts more plays than we even see on the stat sheet.

Nik Bonitto finally gets a sack on 3rd and long with a bull rush to the outside and cutting underneath the tackle as Stafford tried to step up in the pocket. He also chipped in a tackle for loss and 2 quarterback hits.

Eyioma Uwazurike made some noise with his 31 snaps in the game. He forced a holding penalty as he blew by an offensive lineman and was absolutely going to sack Stafford if he didn’t get held. He did get home for one sack, had a tackle for loss, and a quarterback hit.

Justin Strnad made a nice tackle as the back was going by him, wrapping his arm around him and slinging him to the ground. He also had a nice pass break-up in the 3rd quarter, staying precisely on the tight end’s hip. He somehow got matched up on Adams in zone coverage and played absolutely flat-footed, giving him a 40+ yard gain. 

Alex Singleton whiffs a key 3rd down by taking a horrific angle that had a zero percent chance of stopping the receiver. He got picked on in coverage multiple times by Stafford, and rightly so since he’s so slow and vulnerable in one-on-one pass matchups.

Malcolm Roach gets a pass defense by batting down a pass at the LOS. He also chipped in a tackle for loss and a quarterback hit.

I do want to point out that our outside linebacker group isn’t doing enough across from Bonitto. Both Que Robinson and Jonah Elliss have been largely ineffective. It is a shame, as there is a significant opportunity with Jonathan Cooper currently out. They have a real chance to carve out a more significant role in this defense, and neither one seems up to the task.

Secondary

Talanoa Hufanga was the best player on the field on Sunday night, hands down. He did drop a ball thrown directly to his chest and missed another interception that he got his hands on. Both of these indicate that more time on the Juggs machine would serve him well. That being said, he still got 2 interceptions in the game (one of them a pick-6 that was the play of the game). Huff had a superb safety blitz for a big sack in the 4th quarter. Aside from the picks, he had 3 pass defenses in the game as well. The guy was absolutely playing out of his mind, and I love it.

Let’s not be stingy with praise for safeties, though. Brandon Jones absolutely balled out in this game as well. He led the team with 12 tackles on the day, had a tackle for loss, a quarterback hit, and a pass defense. I’m not a big fan of our safeties leading the team in tackles, as that isn’t a good sign, but he was flying to the ball and getting the ball carrier down all game long.

Riley Moss was smothering in his coverage on a crossing route early to get the PD. He gave up an easy pass interference call by holding onto the receiver instead of running with him. He also got absolutely smoked for a touchdown on a double move in the 4th quarter trying to be a hero and force a turnover. It was a rough night for Moss, but thankfully we know he’s pretty great and moving on to the next play.

Speaking of that, Patrick Surtain got some chances to do that over and over in this game. Devonte Adams straight up stole his lunch money in the first half of this game, cooking Surtain for 71 yards on 4 catches. Surtain flipped that script in the 2nd half, allowing Adams only one catch for 6 yards. What an absolute pro shaking off his poor half of play and coming back to being the one doing the cooking in the 2nd half.

Ja’Quan McMillian gave up a big 3rd and 11 by not following the underneath route, thinking he could pass it off to Moss, who was already cleared by another receiver in his zone.

Special Teams 

Kolbe Katsis monster punt return early in the 3rd quarter for 28 yards that flipped the field. He did have a return where he tried running backwards to create space to get to the outside, but that predictably failed. He really helped this team in the return game, averaging 26.8 yards on 4 kickoff returns. With Mims out, I’m glad we have a competent backup to help create those hidden yards that winning teams find.

Wil Lutz missed a makeable field goal trying to kick it straight on instead of angling it just a hair toward the middle of the uprights. Thankfully, it didn’t cost us the win.

Mitchell Frabroni drew a rare snap infraction by picking up the ball and putting it back down without hiking it. Noticing the long snapper typically isn’t a good thing.

Jeremy Crawshaw had another superb punting game with a coffin-corner punt in the 4th quarter that pinned the Rams deep. He had 2 punts inside the 20 and averaged 49.6 yards per punt.

Final Thoughts

Let’s start with the fact that the Broncos beat a very good Rams team on Sunday night. I think they were very fortunate that Puka Nacua and Myles Garrett were out for this game. Nacua alone would have likely changed the outcome of this game.

But you can only play the team in front of you each week. 

There’s a lot of crying about the Rams getting robbed by the very clearly and fairly called pass interference. That’s because the NFL wants drama for that very large LA market. 

What it comes down to is that the Broncos absolutely earned this win. They outplayed the Rams, made another spectacular comeback win in the 4th quarter, and looked like the team that wanted it more in every way. 

This is the tough part of the schedule, and the Broncos, while sloppy, are putting dubs on the board. Being 2-1 after week 3 is a blessing. Now let’s see if we can steal one from the 49ers in San Francisco.

Bo Nix is magic. He’s got Mile High Magic that is undeniable and is the league’s best game-winning 4th-quarter quarterback in the NFL.
