If you are looking for Broncos gear, this is a great way to pick up some quality drip and support the No Bull Review at the same time!

item.title: State of the NFC South: Week 3 recap
item.description: Only one win from the division this weekend
item.content:encoded:
Just when you think you know how the division is going, almost nothing goes as everyone expected.

Tampa Bay Buccaneers

It’s not crazy to say that Bucs HC Todd Bowles could be fired after Week 4. This team has been one of the biggest disappointments in the NFL, and their performance against the Minnesota Vikings was bad. The score showed a 7-point game in the end, but the Bucs made mistakes, and Baker Mayfield struggled. Speaking of Mayfield, near the end of the game, he injured his finger, which looked really bad.

Next week, the Bucs play the Packers, so they could win, but it’s doubtful.

Carolina Panthers

Speaking of shock, the Panthers lost to the Cleveland Browns. First thing, this means the Browns are 2-0 against the NFC South so far. May spell bad news for the rest of the division, but going away from that, let’s focus on this game. The Panthers’ defense didn’t do enough against a Browns offense they should have handled. It doesn’t help that star CB Jaycee Horn went down with an injury and will be out for most of the season.

The offense was also very disappointing and looked nothing like their first two weeks. A performance to forget.

Atlanta Falcons

Somehow, the Falcons are the only winners of the week. After Michael Penix returned, all eyes were on their QB situation, and he did well in his first game. The real hero was Bijan Robinson, who completely controlled this game for Atlanta and gave the Packers zero chance of winning. Could this win be the Packers just being a mess? I actually don’t think so. If Atlanta won by 3 points, then I would say that’s the case, but the Falcons won 35-14.

We are going to see up close what this Falcons team really is, because Atlanta is playing the Saints this week.

New Orleans Saints

And now, a rant I have been waiting for. The Saints’ loss to the Raiders was one of the most frustrating losses since the Drew Brees/Sean Payton era. This game should have been won by New Orleans, and that fourth-quarter collapse was embarrassing. It was really one of the first times the Saints faced adversity while winning, and just like the Ravens last week, they couldn’t recover. The refs had a hand in making that happen, and some of those calls/no calls were truly mind-boggling, but this team had chances to overcome these, and they couldn’t.

It sucks for everyone because I do think many of the Saints’ early weaknesses were fixed in this game. The run game was much better, Taliese Fuaga’s blocking improved, the Saints started fast, the run defense played really well, and the playcalling was exceptional at times. Momentum is a killer, and the Saints fell victim to it. Travis Etienne’s injury is extremely worrying, and the Saints must bring in an RB ahead of this week’s game, but I also think the pass rush needs more talent. This defense had its worst game so far in 2026, and the pass rush behind Chase Young was completely missing. The Saints won’t be able to survive with these two units where they are right now.

NFC South standings:

  1. Carolina Panthers (1-2)
  2. New Orleans Saints (1-2)
  3. Atlanta Falcons (1-2)
  4. Tampa Bay Buccaneers (0-3)

item.title: Buffalo Bills HC Joe Brady wants RB Ray Davis more involved on offense
item.description: Buffalo Bills RB Ray Davis has become a dynamic kick returner, but his potential on offense as a dual-threat player should not go ignored
item.content:encoded:
During Monday’s session at the podium with members of the media, Buffalo Bills head coach Joe Brady took a moment to reflect on running back Ray Davis, and his lack of opportunities in the team’s current offense. Against the Los Angeles Chargers in Week 3, Davis was in for five plays (8%) on offense, while also seeing time on special teams with five plays (22%) there on Sunday.

Davis earned zero touches on those five offensive plays. Meanwhile running back Ty Johnson, just returning to action following a surgical procedure to repair a hamstring injury, saw 15 snaps (23%) on offense, and one snap (4%) on special teams. Johnson didn’t rush the football, but he caught all four targets his way for 50 yards.

Evidenced above, Davis, the 2025 NFL All-Pro kick returner who returned 31 kicks for 943 yards and one touchdown, has a new featured role with Buffalo. Last season while taking over the kick-return reigns, Davis still carried the ball on offense 58 times for 275 yards, also catching 10 passes (13 targets) for 86 yards and two touchdowns.

Running back James Cook III, last season’s NFL rushing yards champion, is the undisputed lead back for the Bills. However, Cook doesn’t take every snap at the position. Despite that fact, Davis has managed to earn just one carry (for 3 yards) through three games this season. It’s surprising when you consider that third-down specialist Ty Johnson missed Weeks 1 and 2.

Are the Bills simply limiting Davis’ touches to keep him fresh for special teams? Perhaps not, as Brady mentioned that “right now, I gotta get Ray playing more, right? Brady went on to say of the situation that ”it’s a reality. He’s too good of a player,” and that ”Ray’s worked his ass off and deserves that” opportunity.

By no means should Cook see less snaps given how productive he is even considering any ball-security concerns. With Cook on the field, the team is always one play away from a sprint going the distance for six. Davis, too, brings a unique ability to the team as someone who’s sneaky fast and tough as nails taking contact. During his rookie season in 2024, Davis totaled 113 carries for 442 yards and three touchdowns, also hauling in 17 receptions (19 targets) for 189 yards and three additional touchdowns.

Be it as it may that Davis has a new role with the team, there’s plenty of room to get him involved meaningfully on offense. He’s a proven dual-threat player who’s succeeded at every stop and each level of football. In Davis’ three-year career to this point with the Bills, he’s averaged a first down on one out of every four rushing attempts (42 first downs, 172 rushes, per Pro Football Reference). As a receiver with the Bills, Davis has earned 15 first downs on 27 receptions (32 targets).

The Bills may be wise to find reason to get Davis snaps in a complementary role to Cook, apart from third-down situations. It could come as soon as Week 4, if there are lingering concerns about the amount and types of contact quarterback Josh Allen continues absorbing as a runner.

item.title: NFL Week 4 Power Rankings: Biggest September Surprises
item.description: Week 4’s WCG NFL Power Rankings are here! After another unpredictable week, there were plenty of shakeups. @AaronLemingNFL has details here.
item.content:encoded:
With Week 3 wrapping up, the NFL will turn the calendar to October as it heads into Week 4. Although the opening month of the season is over, there’s still plenty to learn about all 32 teams around the NFL. Week 2 brought key quarterback injuries, leading to multiple backups making starts and further clouding things for certain teams. With October on the horizon, here’s how our WCG Week 4 Power Rankings shake out. 

1. Buffalo Bills (3-0)

Biggest Surprise Through September: Continuity exists, despite a change at head coach. Is this the boost the Bills needed to get over the hump?

Maybe this isn’t a huge surprise to some, but so far, Joe Brady has his team playing at as high a level as, if not higher than, former head coach Sean McDermott did. Quarterback Josh Allen is the frontrunner for MVP, and for the most part, they’ve looked like the best team in football. 

2. San Francisco 49ers (3-0)

Biggest Surprise Through September: Despite more injuries (no surprise), they are a perfect 3-0, and the defense looks worthy enough to be considered Super Bowl caliber. 

Nick Bosa is hurt again. Their defensive line is in shambles. Mike Evans left with a rib injury on Sunday. Despite that, the 49ers are 3-0, and they look more complete than they did a year ago. There’s no reason to think that won’t continue. 

3. Kansas City Chiefs (3-0)

Biggest Surprise Through September:How quickly a 31-year-old Patrick Mahomes has returned to form is a credit to hard work, and of course, modern medicine. 

Not only are the Chiefs undefeated through September, but their star quarterback looks like he’s back to his normal self. Things got a little dicey against Miami, but Mahomes has a 7-2 touchdown-to-interception ratio, a 68% completion rate, and he’s averaging 270 yards per game. Life is good in Kansas City again.

4. Minnesota Vikings (3-0)

Biggest Surprise Through September: Despite more chaos at quarterback, the Vikings are a perfect 3-0. Will it last? 

Coming back against the Packers at home was one thing. Smoothing a high-scoring Bears offense was another. Now their defense has smothered a third team, and things look great for the Vikings so far in 2026. All of this, despite starting two quarterbacks through three games. All that bad luck from last year appears to be reversed this season. 

5. Seattle Seahawks (2-1)

Biggest Surprise Through September:Their lone loss came with Sam Darnold playing all 60 minutes.

Make no mistake, the Seahawks are one of the best teams in football. They’re also at their best when Darnold is under center. That said, it’s mildly surprising that their only loss of September came with Darnold at quarterback, and with the Jayden Daniels-less Commanders being the ones to do it. 

6. Cincinnati Bengals (2-1)

Biggest Surprise Through September: For the most part, the defense looks Super Bowl caliber. If that holds, the Bengals will be dangerous. 

Even with a disappointing loss to the Steelers on Sunday, fans have to feel good about the direction the Bengals are headed. Dexter Lawrence has helped transform this defense, and if everyone on the offense stays healthy, this will be a team no one wants to face all year. 

7. Baltimore Ravens (2-1)

Biggest Surprise Through September: The defense isn’t quite fixed under first-year head coach Jesse Minter, despite a highly paid and highly talented unit. 

To nobody’s surprise, the offense is back to looking like it normally does with Lamar Jackson under center. First-year offensive coordinator Declan Doyle has done a great job of keeping things explosive. Defensively, they still leave a lot to be desired. While they might be improved, it’s fair to wonder if they’ve improved enough to get back into the Super Bowl contender conversation. 

8. Jacksonville Jaguars (2-1)

Biggest Surprise Through September: The Jaguars and Trevor Lawrence are quickly proving last year’s impressive run wasn’t a fluke. 

Jacksonville was one bad second half against the Broncos from being a perfect 3-0. Head coach Liam Coen became the quickest head coach to 15 wins in franchise history, and for the most part, everything is trending in the right direction. Quarterback Trevor Lawrence can also be included in that conversation. He’s playing at the highest level of his career. 

9. Las Vegas Raiders (3-0)

Biggest Surprise Through September: How real is their hot start? Eventually they’ll turn to Fernando Mendoza, but so far, Kirk Cousins has been more than up to the task. 

The most surprising team in the league through three games? The Las Vegas Raiders at a perfect 3-0 under first-year head coach Klint Kubiak. I’m not sure whether the offense under Cousins or their defense (which has given up just 54 points) has been more impressive. I’m not sure it’ll last, but Raiders fans have to be over the moon heading into October. 

10. Chicago Bears (2-1)

Biggest Surprise Through September: No Caleb Williams… No problem? Despite a disastrous Week 2 that cost the team three to four games with Williams out, Case Keenum helped deliver a winning month.

It would have been easy to write the Bears off after last weekend against Minnesota simply. The offense looked anemic; they lost their starting quarterback, and overall, spirits seemed down heading into a pivotal early-season matchup against the undefeated Eagles. Instead, they have ridden two great defensive performances and a lifetime-from-Keenum performance to come out of September at 2-1 and in good shape moving forward. 

11. Philadelphia Eagles (2-1)

Biggest Surprise Through September: Saquon Barkley is still not himself, and because of that, the Eagles’ offense continues to teeter in the middle.

Despite a 2-0 start, it was easy to look at the quality of their opponents, how they won those games, and wonder what was going on. The defense is no longer elite, but still plenty good enough. Although the offense isn’t “bad” by any stretch of the imagination, it still lacks the same pop we saw from a few years ago. They’re still in good shape moving forward in the NFC East, but it’s worth wondering if Sean Mannion is the answer at offensive coordinator. 

12. Detroit Lions (2-1)

Biggest Surprise Through September: Despite their third new offensive play caller in as many seasons, the Lions’ offense is still pretty damn productive.

It hasn’t looked the same as it did during Ben Johnson’s heyday, but they have scored exactly 31 points in each of their first three games. The bigger concern is the defense, which continues to give up far too many points, leading to a -2 point differential despite averaging 31 points per game offensively. 

13. Denver Broncos (2-1)

Biggest Surprise Through September: Despite being 2-1, offensive regression has hit, and the Broncos have been left searching for consistency. 

Some will blame it on first-year play caller Davis Webb, while others will point to a bad start from quarterback Bo Nix. Regardless of how you cut it, it stands to reason that head coach Sean Payton could take back play-calling if things don’t improve drastically soon for more than one half at a time. We’ll see if they can string together a full game of good offense soon. 

14. Pittsburgh Steelers (2-1)

Biggest Surprise Through September: Despite a new head coach and a 42-year-old quarterback, the Steelers look like a playoff contender.

Count me as shocked as anybody. AFC North games are always close and usually ugly, but being able to pull out a win against the Bengals was an impressive feat. Hell, I’d even argue that it was Aaron Rodgers’ best game of the young season. Now, we’ll see if the offense can do enough to keep them well-rounded. 

15. Los Angeles Rams (1-2)

Biggest Surprise Through September: That vaunted defense won’t be at full strength until at least November. Building continuity while Myles Garrett heals will be key to a deep playoff run.

The Rams came into the regular season as the overwhelming Super Bowl favorites. Yet, the story of the season so far has been Myles Garrett’s injury. Aaron Donald has looked good after a two-year layoff, but without Garrett for the next three-to-four games, they’ll have to find ways to produce pressure and live up to expectations. So far, they are 1-2 in a deep division. 

16. New England Patriots (1-2)

Biggest Surprise Through September: Drake Maye’s fall from grace is extremely concerning. Is this a slow start or something more? 

Through three games, Maye has a 1:6 touchdown-to-interception ratio, and he’s simply not the same quarterback that he was last regular season. Considering his track record last year, logic says he will figure it out. Even so, his knack for mistakes has contributed to their offensive struggles and is a big reason they are 1-2. Buckle up, the schedule doesn’t get any easier any time soon. 

17. DallasCowboys (1-2)

Biggest Surprise Through September: The defense isn’t nearly as good as expected. Will it improve throughout the season? 

All offseason, we heard about the hiring of Christian Parker and all the additions on that side of the ball. Through three games, it hasn’t looked pretty. Week 1 was a disaster, and the end of Week 3’s loss to the Ravens wasn’t much better. Heading into October, they are giving up an average of 27.33 points per game, which isn’t nearly good enough. The talent is there; now we see if they can figure it out. Their season might depend on it. 

18. Green Bay Packers (1-2)

Biggest Surprise Through September: Their -35 point differential tells the story of how much the Packers have struggled to start the year.

Count me as someone who thought the Packers would be worse than most believed. That said, I’m not sure anybody could have predicted this start. Although Micah Parsons has yet to return, even his presence can’t fix all the issues they’ve faced through three games. The immediate concern is stabilizing the offensive line, but the defense has some serious issues too. 

19. New Orleans Saints (1-2)

Biggest Surprise Through September: Tyler Shough is good and, dare I say, the best quarterback from last year’s class?

Now the question is, will that be good enough to win a bad NFC South? They had a prime opportunity to take control of the division in Las Vegas, and despite leading in the fourth quarter, they came up short. Shough is a good, young quarterback, but the rest of the roster needs to come along with him. 

20. New York Giants (2-1)

Biggest Surprise Through September: Jaxson Dart’s season-ending knee injury. Can the Giants stay afloat? 

Any time a team loses an exciting, young quarterback, it’s bad for the league. Combine that with the biggest media market in the country, and it’s an absolute disaster. With Dart done for the year, Jameis Winston led his team to a victory on Sunday. That said, it doesn’t feel overly sustainable for another 14 games, no matter how good a head coach John Harbaugh is. 

21. Indianapolis Colts (1-2)

Biggest Surprise Through September: The defensive struggles, despite the investments on that side of the ball.

Before Week 3’s 17-point performance, the Colts’ defense had given up a combined 74 points over the first two weeks of the season. Considering the investments they have on that side of the ball, it’s a big reason why they find themselves at 1-2. If that improves, life is good. If not, this could finally be the year they clean house. 

22. Carolina Panthers (1-2)

Biggest Surprise Through September: The offensive production. At least through the first two games of the season. Quarterback Bryce Young looks for real, even after a subpar Week 3 performance on the road. 

The good news is that the NFC South is just as bad as it was last year. The bad news is that the Panthers dropped a very winnable game in Cleveland on Sunday. The offense is for real, as is Young, but the defense needs to take bigger strides if it’s going to be better than last year. This division is wide open, but the defense needs to catch up. 

23. Cleveland Browns (2-1)

Biggest Surprise Through September: Deshaun Watson’s best days are behind him, but new head coach Todd Monken seems to have brought out the next best thing. 

Week 2’s win felt like a fluke; Week 3’s win felt like a statement. The defense is still pretty damn good, and frankly, Watson has been considerably better than expected over the last two weeks. Monken is a no-nonsense coach, and his team has embraced that identity so far. 

24. Houston Texans (0-3)

Biggest Surprise Through September: A slow start is one thing; a winless September is another. Concerns are mounting in Houston and for good reason.

On the surface, nothing sticks out as “overly bad,” but they have a 21-point differential and have scored under 20 points in two of their three games. Quarterback C.J. Stroud’s numbers look good on the surface, but their lack of a run game and empty numbers have led to two different disappointing performances through three games. Things need to change, and they need to change fast. 

25. Los Angeles Chargers (0-3)

Biggest Surprise Through September: How is the offense (and Justin Herbert) this bad under Mike McDaniel?

Starting 0-3 is surprising; Herbert and this offense struggling to score points or move the ball is simply shocking. McDaniel was supposed to rebuild his “stock” for a year before taking another head coaching job, but it’s fair to wonder how things look in January if things don’t turn around quickly. People love to make excuses for Justin Herbert, but a 3-4 touchdown-to-interception ratio and a sub-60 % completion rate are unacceptable for a seventh-year quarterback of his caliber. 

26. Washington Commanders (1-2)

Biggest Surprise Through September: Following an 0-2 start, they took down the defending Super Bowl champions with a backup quarterback.

The Commanders, with Marcus Mariota under center, were responsible for Week 3’s biggest upset. Not only did they take down the defending champs, but there’s also a lot to like on defense. Daniels should be back at some point soon, and although it’s unlikely they push for a playoff spot, there’s hope that they can be better than they were last season. 

27. Tampa Bay Buccaneers (0-3)

Biggest Surprise Through September: How are the Buccaneers 0-3? More importantly, it’s fair to wonder how “fixable” it is, even in the lowly NFC South. 

The Bucs have slowly been bleeding talent over the last few years, and it’s fair to wonder if it was smart to extend Baker Mayfield. That said, many could have made a pretty easy argument for them winning the NFC South this season. Instead, they’ve started 0-3, Mayfield dislocated his thumb, and the road doesn’t get any easier in October. 

28. New York Jets (1-2)

Biggest Surprise Through September: The Jets are much more competitive than expected, thanks to a much-improved defense that has still yet to force an interception. 

Even after back-to-back disappointing losses, I’m not sure you’ll find anyone who thinks this group has been anything short of exceeding expectations. Head coach Aaron Glenn still leaves a lot to be desired as an in-game coach, but they’ve finally got some talent, and more will be on the way next offseason. 

29. Atlanta Falcons (1-2)

Biggest Surprise Through September: Tua didn’t start a game, despite Michael Penix missing the first two.

The first two games for the Falcons were disastrous. In fact, their offense didn’t reach the red zone once with Cooper Rush under center. That all changed on Thursday night as they hung 35 points on Green Bay in Penix’s season debut. Despite all the chaos, Tua missed the first two games with back issues and didn’t get a chance to prove himself. That opportunity might be gone now. 

30. Arizona Cardinals (1-2)

Biggest Surprise Through September: They won a game this month and look slightly more competent than expected.

The Cardinals are in the midst of Year 1 of a complete regime change. There’s plenty to rework in the coming years, and although they aren’t likely to win many games, they had the most impressive upset of Week 1. Outside of that, it’s likely to be another long year in Arizona. The only plus is that they finally have a direction. 

31. Tennessee Titans (0-3)

Biggest Surprise Through September: The change at head coach hasn’t yielded the expected results. It’s fair to wonder if quarterback Cam Ward is already on borrowed time. 

Don’t get me wrong: I wasn’t a fan of hiring a defensive-minded head coach for a young quarterback. That said, I believed Ward had enough talent to overcome some early-season hiccups. So far, I’ve been dead wrong. With a new regime at the helm, it’s fair to wonder how long they stick with the plan, especially if they have a high first-rounder come April. 

32. Miami Dolphins (0-3)

Biggest Surprise Through September: The Dolphins might be worse than expected, but without running back De’Von Achane, they could be the shoo-in for the No. 1 overall pick in April. 

It’s no secret that the Dolphins lack talent on both sides of the ball. After all, they are in the infancy stages of a full-blown rebuild. Even so, things have looked ugly. Hence their -50 point differential over three games. With Achane seriously injured, it might be time to start focusing on how they can land the top pick in next year’s draft.

The Daily Slop – 29 September 2026

Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy!

Commanders links

Articles

ESPN

Leo Chenal to have season-ending neck surgery

Washington Commanders linebacker Leo Chenal, who was carted off the field during the team’s 33-31 upset win over the the Seattle Seahawks on Sunday, will undergo season-ending neck surgery, sources confirmed to NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport.

Chenal suffered the injury in the second quarter of Washington’s victory. The fifth-year veteran appeared to lead with his head while tackling Seattle’s Emanuel Wilson and immediately went to the ground as medical personnel were quick to run to his side.

The crowd at Northwest Stadium chanted “Leo! Leo!” as Commanders teammates surrounded Chenal, who was taken off on a cart, raising his left hand as he approached the tunnel.

Chenal was starting Sunday in place of the injured Frankie Luvu, who was missing his second consecutive game with a groin injury.

The Commanders were thin at the position because another inside linebacker, Jordan Magee, was placed on injured reserve after the opener with a hamstring injury.

The Athletic (paywall)

How Commanders rookie Sonny Styles arrived at his NFL breakout: ‘Sonny knows ball’

He is 21. He has played all of three NFL games. Just what did we see from Styles on Sunday in the Commanders’ 33-31 victory over the Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks that, for a week, went a long way to saving Washington’s defense?

“Tremendous leadership,” veteran defensive tackle Tim Settle said of a player in his third pro game. “Tremendous effort. He willed us to a victory today.”

There were all manner of elements that went into this unlikely result. Pick a play that popped, one that sticks in your memory: Terry McLaurin’s brilliant catch of a 30-yard pass from backup quarterback Marcus Mariota that gave Washington a two-touchdown lead in the third quarter. Kain Medrano’s sure-handed snag of an interception at midfield that turned into a rumbling, 50-yard fourth-quarter score. Mariota’s keep on a read-option on third-and-7, a run that gained nine yards and put the game away.

Any of the above — and plenty of others — would be fine choices. But how about Styles, shadowing Seattle rookie running back Jadarian Price out of the backfield?

Washington Post (paywall)

Should the Commanders rush Jayden Daniels back? Not with Marcus Mariota thriving

As good as Mariota looked, there’s no uncertainty about Daniels’s standing. If he’s healthy, he’ll be the starter.

What Mariota’s performance does, however, is allow the Commanders (1-2) to avoid rushing Daniels’s return. They were always going to exercise caution coming off his second elbow dislocation, but this makes it easier to stick to that plan.

Washington will travel to London on Tuesday ahead of Sunday’s game against the Indianapolis Colts (1-2). Although Daniels watched from the sidelines Sunday, it’s unclear whether he will make the trip.

Commanders.com

Mariota’s TD pass to McLaurin was more than what you think

With the Washington Commanders lined up at the Seattle Seahawks’ 30-yard line, Marcus Mariota shuffled to his left and fired a shot to McLaurin near the front of the end zone. McLaurin turned at the last moment, plucked the ball from the air and secured it as he fell to give his team a two-score lead. In the moment, it looked like the play unfolded exactly as the Commanders drew it up.

But that isn’t quite true. The Commanders got the result they wanted, but everything leading up to it was a little different from what they had planned out.

“It kind of changed on the fly,” Mariota said after the game.

McLaurin, known for creating separation at the line of scrimmage, ended up beating cornerback Josh Jobe so cleanly that it made more sense for him to run a go route. McLaurin trusted that Mariota would recognize the change, and sure enough, the quarterback put the ball in a spot where only McLaurin could make the catch.

“We don’t try to make a habit of going off key, but at the end of the day, we speak about being ball players out there,” McLaurin said. “When you get a clean release like that, and you have a chance to make a big play, you want to capitalize, and we did that.”

Commanders notebook: Does Jayden Daniels returning to practice mean Dan Quinn will be calling his name in London?

Washington will hold a lighter practice Wednesday in London before ramping up the workload Thursday and Friday. Quinn indicated those later sessions should provide the clearest indication of how close Daniels is to returning.

“Just the fact that we’re working back into that space gives me optimism heading into the week about where we’re at and the health of the team,” Quinn said.

Sports Illustrated

Washington Put More on Amik Robertson Against Seattle

[Robertson played] 65 of 67 snaps while recording six tackles, four passes defensed, forcing the Jadarian Price fumble that Tim Settle recovered and led to Washington’s first score a few plays later. Jones told them to keep chopping; Robertson was the guy who finally knocked the tree down.

To be clear, Robertson has done well all season; his six PBUs (pass breakups) rank first overall among qualifying corners through Week 3. Pro Football Focus has him ranked third in several categories, including an 88.5 overall grade, an 89.3 coverage grade, and an 85.6 run defense grade. His six passes defensed are already half of what he had in all of 2025.

To read more of this article, CLICK HERE

Bullock’s Film Room (subscription)

Commanders Film Review: Amik Robertson vs Seahawks

[Note: The play discussed in this excerpt is the one in the tweet embedded below]

Perhaps the best of Robertson’s pass break ups was his third one, when he was working against Seahawks star receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba.

On this play, Robertson lines up opposite Smith-Njigba, one of the best receivers in the NFL, if not the best receiver outright. Smith-Njigba runs a slant route on second and 14 to try and give Darnold an easy completion that can get the Seahawks into a more manageable third down situation. Robertson initially lines up on the line of scrimmage but bails out deeper just before the snap.

This is the type of play this defense wants it’s cornerbacks to make. The idea of this defense is to blitz a ton, generate pressure and force the offense into quick passes underneath to avoid getting sacked. Things like slants and quick outs are what teams go to against pressure, so the cornerbacks are trained to sit about eight to 10 yards off and trigger on anything underneath aggressively. The Commanders don’t bring pressure here but the response from Robertson is the right one. Smith-Njigba breaks inside on the slant and Robertson immediately triggers on it.

Because of that quick trigger, Robertson makes up the distance between them and as the ball arrives, Robertson gets his hand in at the catch point to break it up yet again, setting up a third and long situation that heavily favors the defense. That’s exactly the type of quick, aggressive trigger on an underneath route that this defense should thrive on. We saw Sainristil hesitate in a similar situation last week against the Cowboys, but Robertson had no such hesitation and was rewarded with his third pass break up of the game.

While that play was perhaps his most impressive one, Robertson’s fourth break up was perhaps his most important.

Metro Sports Page: A sixpack of the Mondays

Commanders Look to Build Momentum After 0-2 Start

By Ken Meringolo

Welcome to the first Victory Sixpack of the new year! With a win over the defending Super Bowl champions, the Washington Commanders put a hard stop to the Seattle Seahawks’ winning streak and breathed just a little bit of hope and life into the 2026 season. Going 1-2 to start the campaign might not sound like the accomplishment it feels like it is today, but this schedule we spent all summer lamenting has started out every bit as hard as we feared. Adding to the degree of difficulty,of course, are the players unable to suit up for us already in the early stages of the year. I don’t think I was alone in my–worry–that it could have been a little bit of a wait for that first win of the season. Yesterday’s 33-31 win was a strong NFC conference win (making us 1-2 in the NFC after three weeks), but it was also the kind of win that could allow us to reset some expectations for the next month of the season.

We learned that no team had more new players snapping for a defense than the Commanders over the first two weeks. That is why we covered snap counts after week one–and it was a clear takeaway. I know Adam Peters has taken some shrapnel over the last few months as people have drilled into granular performance data on his draft picks and free-agent acquisitions, but on a rainy and blustery day in Landover, Peters gave a strong rebuttal. In addition to solid games from Amik Robertson and Tim Settle, two non-sexy offseason free-agent pickups, when it came time to attempt to recover from losing Leo Chenal, we had an Adam Peters deep cut ready to go in Kain Medrano. To be fair, all of Peters’ picks have not been home runs, but yesterday his 2025 draft class really shined, with Josh Conerly Jr., Jaylin Lane and Jacory Croskey-Merritt all joining Medrano to contribute to the win.

The Commanders have a chance on Sunday to string together some wins…back-to-back victories would do wonders not just for postseason chances, but for the confidence of so many new and young players in burgundy and gold. You can make your team younger by signing younger players and releasing older players (Kevin had a great PowerPoint presentation on this math). You can get younger and faster the same way. However, you can only build a winning culture by…winning. On the road and across the pond (technically a home game), our Commanders have a chance to help this new batch of players build something truly meaningful in sports: momentum.

ESPN

Big loss for Seattle Seahawks on visit to Washington

The champs were riding a 12-game winning streak and hadn’t lost in 314 days. J.J. McCarthy traded to Giants: Will he succeed in New York?

Landing a fifth-round pick for McCarthy was an obvious call for the Vikings. Once their quarterback of the future after they traded up to take him in the first round of the 2024 draft, McCarthy had quickly and brutally fallen out of favor in Minnesota. After being the NFC Offensive Player of the Week in his NFL debut last season — an opening-week win over the Bears — McCarthy’s inability to work all areas of the field, operate within the structure of the offense or avoid negative plays frustrated a Vikings organization that had let Sam Darnold leave in free agency to hand the job to him.

While it was no surprise when McCarthy lost something resembling a QB competition to new starter Kyler Murray in training camp this summer, the writing was really on the wall once it became clear that Kevin O’Connell preferred Carson Wentz as his second option. Trading McCarthy netted some small amount of draft capital for the Vikings while also saving them $4.6 million over the next two years in the process.

So, the trade makes sense for both organizations. Will it work out for McCarthy, who is still only 23 years old and younger than Ty Simpson, whom the Rams took with their first-round pick in this year’s draft? We’re living in a bit of a golden era of second (or third) acts for quarterbacks around the NFL, with the likes of Darnold, Bryce Young, Malik Willis, Baker Mayfield and others enjoying varying levels of success after their first organization gave up (and/or benched) them before the end of their rookie deals. Could McCarthy be the next to follow in their footsteps and turn his career around after a rough start?

[O]ver his final four starts in 2025, McCarthy was quietly … pretty good? Returning from a concussion, he oversaw four victories as the Vikings worked their way back to respectability over the end of the year. And over that stretch, McCarthy wasn’t a problem for the Minnesota offense. He completed 64.3% of his passes, averaged a robust 8.4 yards per attempt and threw five touchdown passes against two picks, adding two more scores with his legs. McCarthy’s sack rate dropped to 7.7%, which is still higher than you would like but much improved on what he had produced early in the season.

Those aren’t superstar numbers, but the McCarthy of the first six games was one of the worst QBs we’ve seen over the past decade, whereas the guy over the final four starts was completely playable. His 70.3 Total QBR over that stretch was the seventh-best mark in the league, just behind Matthew Stafford, who was finishing up an MVP season for the Rams. He was fourth in yards per dropback and eighth in passer rating.

He hasn’t been healthy enough to stay on the field for any meaningful stretch of time. He missed all of his rookie year after tearing his meniscus, which required season-ending surgery. He was then sidelined for seven games in 2025 amid a high-ankle sprain, a concussion and a hand injury. It’s unclear whether McCarthy would have beaten Darnold out for the job as a rookie in 2024, but he was healthy enough to start 10 of 34 possible contests over his first two seasons in the league before the Vikings moved on to Murray this offseason.

You can’t develop as a quarterback if you can’t stay on the field to get regular reps. And while McCarthy was relatively healthy during his time under Jim Harbaugh at Michigan, he has yet to make it to a fifth consecutive start as a pro without getting hurt. The Giants were already worried about this with Dart, and now they’re acquiring a second quarterback who hasn’t been able to stay healthy or protect himself as a pro.

The numbers from that four-game stretch in 2025 are real, but they come with some incredibly large qualifiers. That run started against the Commanders, who fielded the league’s second-worst defense by QBR. It continued against the Cowboys (fourth-worst) and then these Giants (10th-worst). And it finished with the Packers, who would have been the league’s second-worst defense by QBR if we just consider their snaps without Micah Parsons on the field. (The star edge rusher missed that Week 18 matchup with the Vikings after tearing his ACL.) Total QBR adjusts for quality of opposition, but that’s a particularly friendly slate of opponents.

Even in those games, the Vikings very clearly didn’t trust McCarthy. They dialed up designed runs nearly 46% of the time, which would have been the fifth-most run-heavy offense in the NFL. The Vikings asked McCarthy to throw only 21 passes per game over that stretch, a barely-there workload for most quarterbacks, albeit one more in line with how rarely McCarthy threw at Michigan (22 times per contest). Minnesota played at the third-slowest pace in the league to try to shorten games and lean heavily on the defense, which was both smart and likely telling about how the team viewed McCarthy.

Obviously, if there’s something more here and he turns into a solid NFL starter, this would be a heist for the Giants in the big picture.

You just really have to squint and be incredibly selective about what you leave out to have any optimism about McCarthy given what we saw from him in 2025. Even guys like Darnold and Young weren’t as bad early in their careers as McCarthy was in 2025, and they were much more impactful college passers in terms of their responsibilities.

[A]s we saw a year ago, the floor for what he might offer as a quarterback can be painful to watch. I can’t fault the Giants for trying to do something, given Dart’s injury, but I would be very surprised if McCarthy was any sort of short- or long-term answer for this organization.

item.description: Penalties nearly cost the Longhorns a victory on Saturday.
item.content:encoded:
Things have quickly turned downhill on the penalty front for the No.1 Texas Longhorns. After six penalties for 47 yards in the first two games, the Longhorns have been flagged 19 times for 203 yards in the last two games, including a maddening 11-penalty, 115-yard meltdown in the 20-17 win over the Tennessee Volunteers this past Saturday.

“We’ve got to find ways to clean up the penalties,” Texas head coach Steve Sarkisian said on Monday. “Now it’s 19 penalties in the last two weeks and we can control a lot of them. Some of them we can’t. We can control a lot of them. So again, we’ve got to get back to the emphasis as a coaching staff.”

The frequency, impact, and foolishness of the 11 penalties were head scratching. Time and time again, the Longhorns found new and creative ways to shoot themselves in the foot. For a team with legitimate College Football Playoff aspirations, games like this cannot keep happening.

Tennessee’s only successful offensive drive in the first 56 minutes of game resulted in a field goal thanks to 30 free yards from the Texas defense. Defensive end Lance Jackson, who played exceptionally well for a majority of the game, was called for roughing the passer on the first play of the series, which promptly moved the Volunteer offense from their own 25-yard line to the Texas 49-yard line.

Two plays later, cornerback Bo Mascoe was flagged for pass interference, granting Tennessee 15 more yards. The drive resulted in a field goal, a win for the defense considering that 30 of the 60 yards were self-inflicted penalty yards.

Mascoe was ultimately flagged twice on the day for pass interference, upping the secondary’s total tally to four on the year as fellow defensive back Kade Phillips has been called for pass interference twice himself.

“I thought one I could understand PI, the other one I thought he played it pretty well,” Sarkisian said.

Quarterback Arch Manning also had a tough day with the zebras. Twice, and for the third team in the last two games, Manning threw a forward pass while beyond the line of scrimmage. It’s a rather bizarre penalty and hurt the Longhorns both times given that it is a loss of down.

“The first one, I think he thought he was getting it off before the line to gain,” Sarkisian said. “I actually think on the second one we were in, I believe a 3rd and 12, and I think he was operating off the 1st and 10 marker, not the stripe that was actually where we were. So, I guess it can happen that way.”

The order of the plays was reversed, but the impact remained.

Running back Raleek Brown was open early on the first illegal forward pass and would have had an easy first down to convert 3rd and 12. Instead, Texas punted, and an illegal formation penalty on the punt allowed Tennessee to take over at its own 42-yard line.

The second illegal forward pass was a 2nd and 15 on which Manning didn’t have any room to scramble and should have thrown the ball away earlier.

Manning was also called for a delay of game in the third quarter that turned a 3rd and 2 into a 3rd and 7 that led to a field goal as Texas missed a chance to convert a short-yardage play in a potential four-down situation.

The most documented penalty was an unsportsmanlike call on edge Colin Simmons. The post-sack celebration caught the attention of the entire country and cost the Longhorns, but ultimately didn’t impact the final score. His choice to celebrate in that manner is totally avoidable and the type of penalty that demonstrates an undisciplined team.

Special teams was penalized multiple times for the second week in a row, including the illegal formation and, more consequentially, Ryan Niblett had a return to midfield negated thanks to a block in the back that turned a 14-yard return into a four-yard return. Texas went three and out on the drive when Manning was forced to recover a bad snap that resulted in a 12-yard loss on first down.

Though not a penalty, another sizable punt return was also called back, neutralizing the ability for the Longhorns to start the drive in opposing territory instead of at their own 32-yard line. Texas went three and out.

The final penalty on the sloppy day was a huge face mask with 26 seconds left in the game as Simmons recorded a sack on 3rd and 19 that turned into a first down on the penalty against defensive end Zina Umeozulu.

It’s difficult to point fingers when a player is simply trying to make things happen, especially in the trenches, but the penalty extended the game and could have resulted in disaster.

As a whole, Texas finished with penalties of all varieties. Offense, defense, and special teams contributed. There were calls before the snap, during the play, and after the whistle. Mental miscues and repeat offenders all played a role.

So, while the the Horns ultimately escaped with a win, the trend regarding penalties is growing increasingly alarming. Last week’s disappointing reversal is tough to dismiss as a fluke after Saturday. If the Longhorns hope to remain unbeaten, getting back to disciplined play is required — last two weeks are not sustainable moving forward.

Texas is now down to 90th nationally in penalty yards per game at 62.5. And although the Longhorns rank much higher in penalties per game, that only indicates how much damage the penalties they’ve committed produced in terms of total yardage.

With a bye this week, Texas has a chance to regroup before facing Oklahoma in Dallas on October 10th at 2:30 p.m. Central.

item.content:encoded:
Monday night's game between the Eagles and Bears featured a moment in which former Eagles (now Bears) linebacker T.J. Edwards tiptoed toward the huddle to try to hear what Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts was saying.

Then the play started, and Edwards intercepted a pass from Hurts.

After the game, Edwards was asked whether he picked anything up from his eavesdropping attempt.

"No," Edwards said, via Kevin Fishbain of The Athletic. "I was like, 'Maybe I'll hear some familiar stuff,' and like they must have changed language up because I had no idea what they were talking about."

That's no surprise. Edwards last played for the Eagles in 2022. They've had four offensive coordinators since Edwards left.

Regardless, Edwards brings to the Bears a knowledge of Hurts and other players with whom he played. It's one of the basic realities of today's high-mobility NFL. Little things can be picked up and possibly used later. Tendencies, tells, habits, etc.

Every quarterback needs to be keeping notes on all defenders he faces in practice, and every defender needs to be keeping notes on all quarterbacks they face in practice. Today's coworker can be tomorrow's enemy, and an edge can come from anywhere.

item.title: Nebraska Football Player Power Rankings: A New #1 and the Five-Star Who Finally Showed Up
item.description: Nebraska if 4-0 and Anthony Colandrea is a big reason why. So he gets the #1 spot this week.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to the most recent edition of my Nebraska Football player power rankings. As I have said before, this list will be completely subjective in several ways and may not follow a logical path. Or maybe it will.

This Power Ranking list will be a combination of the most important, most impactful, a recent contribution, waiting in the wings, rumors of greatness, rumors of not-so-great, players that made one great play to change a game (for better or worse) or any other type of metric that I think should go with this subjective list.

So without further ado, here is my most recent definitive and completely subjective Nebraska Football Player Power Ranking.

Here are links to prior Nebraska Football Player Power Rankings.

Start of Fall Camp
Halfway through Fall Camp
Week One: Ohio
Week Two: Bowling Green
Week Three: North Dakota
Week Four: Michigan State

The List

10. Jacory Barney Jr., Wide Receiver

Prior Ranking: 6th

Jacory Barney caught one pass and fumbled it. Luckily Justin Evans jumped on it.

Barney left the game with an apparent injury though at this time we do not know if he’ll be back for Maryland or if this is a long term issue.

Yesterday Head Coach Matt Rhule said he would be surprised if Barney isn’t back because “he’s made of rubber.”

9. Jamal Rule, Running Back

Prior Ranking: 4th

I think there were a couple of runs before Jamal Rule got hurt that made me think “welcome to the Big Ten freshman.”

I think that experience will be great for Rule as he is clearly the most talented running back in the room. He only played eight snaps but he gets to hang out in the Top 10 because of the work he did prior to the Michigan State game.

The fact that he came out of the locker-room and was doing sprints on the sideline to test his ankle makes me think that he could go this week but maybe the staff might want to wait a week and get a healthy Jamal Rule against Indiana.

Nebraska is favored by 12-14 points this week against Maryland. The Terrapins were blown out by UCLA this past week (54-3) so maybe Rhule is thinking he could rest Jamal Rule to get him ready for Indiana. However, we know that football coaches do not think that way. It’s hard to win games in college football.

8. Luke Lindenmeyer, Tight End

Prior Ranking: 9th

Lindenmeyer was targeted five times and caught four passes. They tried to get him a touchdown on the goal line but were unsuccessful.

But Lindenmeyer continues to go “head hunting” as I saw him getting knockdown after knockdown. He is almost like a kid in youth baseball that is getting paid a dollar per base they make. He’s going after those knockdowns like he’s getting paid for it.

Which is great.

7. Andrew Marshall, Defensive Back

Prior Ranking: 8th

One of my favorite aspects of the play-by-play of Marshall’s interception against Michigan State is how disappointed they sound. They were probably hoping that Michigan State would score a touchdown on that drive (6:48 left in the fourth quarter) to make it a game but Marshall shut the door on that hope. 

Marshall had his highest graded game of the season by PFF at 79.8.


6. Williams Nwaneri, Defensive Lineman

Prior Ranking: Unranked

I think the five-star defensive lineman has finally arrived. On Monday, Matt Rhule was very hesitant to anoint Nwaneri but after two sacks against Michigan State and a blocked kick, we are starting to finally see what we thought we were getting when he transferred from Missouri. 

I loved his quote from the post-game press conference – “(Defensive coordinator Rob Aurich) said to make the quarterback see ghosts.”

5. Donovan Jones, Defensive Back

Prior Ranking: 10th

Sometimes real good players make real good plays. Jones has two sacks over the past two games on some timely blitzes. Against Michigan State, he got the strip sack fumble and then jumped off the ground to recover the fumble. 

Apparently going into the season he was considered the second best NFL prospect on the Nebraska roster and we are starting to see why. 

On his forced fumble against Michigan State, I thought the quarterback was was already down, but Jones still forced and recovered the fumble.

4. Kwazi Gilmer, Wide Receiver

Prior Ranking: 7th

Gilmer is starting to remind me a little bit of Trey Palmer with his ability to take the top off the defense. He’s leading the team in receptions and yards. He also has done a great job of blocking down the field. But this gives me the opportunity to tell the following boring story.

My internet went out at the worst time on Saturday.

It happened as Nebraska’s offense went three-and-out for the second straight possession. Michigan State just went up 3-0 on a field goal and we were ready to give them the ball back. What was definitely going to happen (as we have seen this before) is that Michigan State is going to get the ball back and score a touchdown. They would be up 10-0 and then it’s Pat Fitzgerald time and they would drain the clock the rest of the game.

I thought our only chance to beat Michigan State was to get an early lead and force them to throw the ball. So here we are as Nebraska is about to snap the ball to Archie Wilson and then boom, my internet went out.

A few minutes later it came back and we are up 7-3.

I literally started texting my friends saying “what the _____ just happened?”

What I also did not realize until a couple hours after the game is that the punt that I missed was actually blocked. Luckily Nebraska got the benefit of a holding penalty before the 44-yard touchdown pass to Kwazi Gilmer.


3. Justin Evans, Center

Prior Ranking: 1st

The Nebraska offense had trouble running the ball against Michigan State and the offensive line as a whole had their worst day of the season so far according to their PFF ratings. Still Justin Evans is considered one of the best centers in the country and I think they will get the run game figured out.

Justin Evans also made one of the biggest plays of the game. It ended up being a 17 yard “completion” from Colandrea to Jacory Barney but it was actually a shorter pass that Barney then fumbled.

But it was Justin Evans running down the field to be in position to jump on that fumble at the Michigan State 17-yard line. This was the play right after the Owen Chambliss interception. Nebraska ends up kicking a field goal to go up 17-3.

2. Owen Chambliss, Linebacker

Prior Ranking: 3rd

Owen Chambliss is going to get a lot of credit when the defense plays well. He is going to get even more credit when he drops into coverage and is in the right place at the right time for the interception.

Chambliss also had one of the best graded games according to PFF with a 72.8 and played 55 snaps. His tackling grade was an 83.8 which was great.

I hope he stays healthy because the defense just looks different when he’s out there.

1. Anthony Colandrea, Quarterback

Prior Ranking: 2nd

I know that I am not alone in thinking that if Anthony Colandrea was not our quarterback against Michigan State the game likely ends as a one score win or a one score loss.

Even with all of the timely penalties and turnovers by Michigan State it was Colandrea that was able to get from pressure or escape from the pocket to run for first downs on second and third and long. He did it at least three times to extend the drive against the Spartans.

There were several plays which would have been sacks last year which ended up in either an incompletion at worst or a chunk play at best. 

Through four games he has not turned the ball over once (admittedly he was credited with an interception but we know that was not his fault). 

I think the offense and the defense both gain confidence from knowing that he is back there at quarterback. Hopefully he can learn to slide from time to time so he can stay healthy.

item.title: Fantasy Football Panic Meter, Week 4: Which Year 2 RBs are we most worried about?
item.description: Ray Garvin goes over players he's worried about going into Week 4 for fantasy football.
item.content:encoded:
Three weeks into the fantasy season, the excuses start getting a little harder to make. One bad game? Fine. Two games? We can still talk ourselves into patience. By Week 4, though, we have enough information to start asking whether what we drafted is actually what we have.

For running backs, I care about more than just touches. Seventeen carries can look great in a box score, but what kind of carries are they? Is the player involved on third down? Is he catching passes? Is he getting the football near the goal line? Is the offense creating enough scoring opportunities?

That is where this week's Panic Meter starts.

The thresholds remain the same: No Panic, Some Panic, Total Panic or Coping Corner. All four of these Year 2 running backs have disappointed in some way. They just haven't disappointed for the same reasons.

Omarion Hampton: SOME PANIC

The carries keep pulling me back in with Omarion Hampton. Almost everything else is pushing his ceiling away.

Through three games, Hampton has 50 carries for 193 yards and two touchdowns. That is enough volume to keep him playable. The problem lies in the kind of work he is getting.

Hampton caught 32 passes in only nine games as a rookie. Through three games this season, he has two catches on three targets. Alec Ingold caught three passes for 35 yards in Week 3 alone. Hampton has fewer receptions through three weeks than his fullback had in one game.

Week 3 made the concern worse. Hampton played just 27 of 64 snaps and ran six routes. Keaton Mitchell played 23 snaps and ran 15 routes while Kimani Vidal handled much of the obvious passing-down work. Hampton saw only one of seven running back targets.

The Chargers are starting to split this backfield into three jobs. Hampton is the primary early-down runner, Mitchell gives them speed and Vidal is taking valuable passing-down snaps. That strips away the receiving ceiling fantasy managers were counting on.

The offense is not helping either. Los Angeles is 0-3 and has scored 14, 14 and 16 points, respectively. Even a secure goal-line role only goes so far when the team rarely gets there.

I'm at Some Panic. Hampton is still averaging more than 17 touches per game and has handled 50 of the Chargers' 68 running back carries, so the floor is still there. What has changed is the ceiling.

Fantasy managers drafted a three-down breakout and right now, all they have is an early-down volume back.

Ashton Jeanty: SOME PANIC

Ashton Jeanty represents almost the opposite problem.

The role is excellent. He has 76 touches through three games, 63 carries and 16 targets, and he played 83% of the snaps in Week 3. If you showed me that workload in August, I would have loved it.

But the production has not matched it.

Jeanty has 206 rushing yards on 63 carries — just 3.3 yards per attempt — with no rushing touchdowns. After opening with 102 yards on 23 carries, he has 104 rushing yards on 40 carries over the last two weeks. He also dropped three passes in Week 2 and failed on two early goal-line carries.

What has stood out most is the lack of the tackle-breaking and explosive rushing we saw from him as a rookie.

Mike Washington Jr. gave us a sharp contrast in Week 3. Jeanty's longest run on 19 carries was 12 yards. Washington turned five carries into 54 yards, including a 36-yard touchdown.

I'm not worried about Washington stealing the backfield. He played only 17% of the snaps. I'm worried because Jeanty is getting everything we want from a workload perspective and still has not consistently looked like the player fantasy managers paid for.

Las Vegas is 3-0 and averaging 29.3 points per game. The offense is creating scoring chances. Jeanty has two receiving touchdowns and still averages 18.4 PPR points, but the 32.7-point opener is carrying a lot of that number. Since then, he has scored 10.3 and 12.3, respectively.

So I'm staying at Some Panic. The workload is too strong to increase the panic level, but I need the explosive plays and tackle-breaking to return before I'm comfortable viewing Jeanty as the elite difference-maker fantasy managers drafted.

Quinshon Judkins: NO PANIC

Quinshon Judkins has not been good. He also has not given me a reason to change the evaluation.

Through three games, Judkins has 42 carries for 124 yards, nine receptions for 53 yards and no touchdowns. He is averaging 3.0 yards per carry. Nobody drafted him expecting efficiency to carry his fantasy value.

His value comes from owning Cleveland's rushing work, and that part remains intact.

Judkins handled 18 of the Browns' 19 running back carries in Week 3 and finished with 70 rushing yards. Raheim Sanders took some passing-down work while Cleveland was chasing points late, but Sanders has only four carries all season. Jaleel McLaughlin barely played and Dylan Sampson is on injured reserve.

The setup is pretty straightforward. Judkins controls the early-down rushing work in an offense averaging 18 points per game. The receiving ceiling is limited and touchdown opportunities are going to determine a lot of his better fantasy weeks.

For me, that stays at No Panic.

That doesn't mean I love the profile. It means the usage still matches the reason you drafted him. He is a volume-based RB2 or flex who can give you 15 to 20 touches and needs touchdowns to push beyond that. Three games have not changed the player or the role enough for me to react.

TreVeyon Henderson: TOTAL PANIC

TreVeyon Henderson is the one I am most concerned about. He missed Week 1 with an ankle injury, returned in Week 2 and immediately gave fantasy managers hope with 16 carries for 76 yards and a touchdown.

Then Week 3 pulled the rug back out.

Henderson played 21 snaps to Rhamondre Stevenson's 32. Henderson had a narrow 9-8 edge in carries, but Stevenson led 3-1 in targets and handled more of the passing-down work. Across Henderson's two active games, he has 25 touches to Stevenson's 18, but Henderson has only one target.

So yes, Henderson can lead this backfield in carries and still lose the snaps that carry more fantasy value.

Now, put that role inside a Patriots offense averaging 12 points per game. New England has scored 36 points in three weeks, the offensive line is dealing with injuries and Drake Maye has struggled to keep the offense on schedule. Henderson is being asked to create fantasy value without a reliable receiving role or control of the backfield.

We know he can create explosive plays. He averaged 5.1 yards per carry as a rookie, rushed for 911 yards and scored four touchdowns of at least 50 yards.

The problem is how much he needs those plays right now.

You cannot build a weekly fantasy expectation around waiting for a 40-yard run. That is Total Panic for me. The talent is still there, but the role is not strong enough and the offense is not producing enough points to cover for it.

Henderson can still save your week with one play, but New England is giving him very little else.

item.title: NFL Power Rankings for Week 4: Denver Broncos enter the top five after comeback win
item.description: The Denver Broncos are the most dangerous team in the NFL. How so? Because no team does what they do when down multiple scores in the second half.
item.content:encoded:
The Denver Broncos have earned a reputation for being the comeback kings of the NFL after doing it in back-to-back weeks. They won so many of those types of games last season that most assumed they would be due for a reversion to the mean in 2026. So far, that hasn’t been the case. This team thrives off the high pressure, high stakes of a comeback.

The power rankings are a mixed bag because of that. They rose across the board, but some prognosticators only moved them slightly still doubting their ability to keep up the comeback game. However, plenty do believe and the move was significant and into the Top 5 overall.

Frankly, I don’t know if they can keep this up. But I do know I’m enjoying the ride and enjoying the Bo Nix experience. It’s not quite like Tebow Time. It’s a lot more like John Elway with a hint of Tebow, because some of these comebacks are just too insane not to think of Tebow.

Here’s how the Broncos are doing in this week’s power rankings around the web:

CBS Sports – 6th

Coming back to win games late is their calling card. They did it again against the Rams Sunday night, but that’s playing with fire on a weekly basis.

NBC Sports – 4th

The Rams let the Broncos hang around just long enough to steal it.

ESPN – 6th

The Broncos’ offensive struggles, especially in first halves, have dragged down everybody’s numbers. They haven’t found a rhythm much of the time, and save for Jaylen Waddle’s 138-yard effort against the Jaguars in Week 2, the WRs have been caught up in the wash (Pat Bryant has the group’s only TD catch). Sutton, who is second in targets to Waddle with 16, could be seen as the biggest disappointment. He has yet to eclipse more than 10 fantasy points in any game.

New York Times – 4th

Bo Nix is 26-11 as Denver’s starter, which gives him eight more wins than any other member of the 2024 quarterbacks class. So Broncos fans aren’t interested in hearing about how he’s 30th in the league in EPA per dropback (minus-0.14) and 26th in touchdown-to-interception ratio (4-to-3). Denver scored as many points in the second half Sunday as it did in the first 10 quarters of the season combined, so maybe Nix and offensive coordinator Davis Webb are figuring each other out.

USA Today – 5th

They’ve been 10 points better on the scoreboard every week, meaning they’re on pace to score 40 at San Francisco on Sunday. Maybe. Yet for all the scrutiny that’s followed new OC Davis Webb, it’s the defense that’s really underachieved here so far. A team that averaged four sacks per game in 2025 is currently at 2.67.

Fox Sports – 3rd

They had a second half for the ages against the Rams, maybe with a little help from the officials. If they could just get QB Bo Nix and their offense going a little sooner, they’d be a scary team. But they certainly have the defense to play against anyone, and Sean Payton may be the best coach in the NFL when his team is playing from behind. They’ve already come from behind twice to win this year. 

And yes, I know they were blitzed by the Chiefs in Week 1, and they are still ranked ahead of them. These are power rankings, not standings. Thanks for your continued concern.

What do you think of these power rankings? Share in the comments section below!

item.title: Eagles-Bears takeaway: Lackluster play catches up with the Birds in Chicago
item.description: It was a brutal night in Chicago on Monday night for Jalen Hurts and the Birds.
item.content:encoded:
You could feel this game coming.

In Week 1, the Eagles struggled to beat the Commanders in Washington 24-22. They followed it up with a last-second, 24-20 victory on the road against the Titans, who finished with the NFL’s second-worst record a season ago.

The defense had put together two lackluster performances against weaker opponents. The offense was bailed out by Jalen Hurts playing hero ball.

And so last night’s 27-7 shellacking at the hands of Ben Johnson’s Bears in Chicago shouldn’t have been too surprising.

Hopefully, it’s a wake-up call.

Against an opponent superior to the two they played previously, Hurts couldn’t paper over the offensive line’s continuing and worrisome struggles, and the defensive line’s inability to pressure the quarterback continued despite the return of Jonathan Greenard. Meanwhile, the secondary suffered breakdowns throughout the game and allowed a third-string QB who they beat in the… checks notes… 2017 NFC Championship Game put up a 110.8 rating against them.

Yup, that was the same Case Keenum throwing for 247 yards, 2 TDs and no interceptions against a Vic Fangio unit that garnered a whole lotta hype in training camp. They’ve given up an average of 23.0 points per game through three outings, 16th in the NFL. They have three sacks thus far and have yet to force a turnover, sitting -5 in the turnover differential. Per Sumer Sports, the Birds are 23rd in EPA/play and 20th in success rate.

The safeties and linebacking corps haven’t looked good through three games. Drew Mukuba, Marcus Epps and Michael Carter II have missed tackles and blown assignments. Nakobe Dean’s absence has been felt, with Jihaad Campbell so far failing to replicate his predecessor’s performance. But the real issue stems from the defensive line, who quite simply, hasn’t delivered on their preseason promise.

A lot of money has been invested on the defensive line. Jalen Carter signed a 4-year, $152 million contract extension with $107 million in guaranteed money this off-season. Jordan Davis got a 3-year, $78 million deal with $64 million guaranteed. Jonathan Greenard received a 4-year, $98 million extension after his trade from Minnesota, and Jalyx Hunt will likely be the next lineman to follow with a similar mega-deal.

Greenard just this week returned to the field following two weeks on the injured list, so it’s unfair to expect peak performance from him as of yet, but there is little excuse for everyone else. Moro Ojomo and Nolan Smith, two young players looking to secure big deals of their own, have been largely silent.

One has to think Fangio’s guys will figure this out and get it together, but there is absolutely no excuse for getting shredded in a prime time NFL game by Case Keenum in the year 2026. A defense some believed would be one of the five best units in the sport has been middling through their first three games, and the onus is on the defensive line to make life difficult for opposing coordinators.

On the offensive side, preseason concerns about the O-line were well-founded.

Landon Dickerson’s inability to return to full health was less than ideal. Fortunately, last year’s 5th-round pick Drew Kendall has held his own thus far at center. The rest of the line has struggled.

Tyler Steen has been abysmal at right guard to start the season. Cam Jugens, who shifted from center to left guard with Dickerson out, can’t find any consistency. And Jordan Mailata, one of the highest-priced vets on the team, has simply not been the same player since the 2024 Super Bowl season. Lane Johnson has been fine at right tackle, but he can’t do it all alone.

On 1st-and-goal from just outside the one yard line in the 2nd quarter, the offensive line couldn’t generate enough push or open up a single lane to allow Barkley to run the ball into the end zone for the tying score. Instead, they forced Sean Mannion to try a pass play on 3rd-and-goal from the 2 with Andy Dalton, who threw an interception in the end zone.

A 95-yard drive ended in no points as a result.

Sure, Dalton is terrible, should not be on the roster and should not have been asked to throw a pass in that situation. But the O-line’s inability to get Barkley in the end zone on first and second downs shouldn’t be ignored, either.

In the first half against the Bears, the line looked like it was figuring things out. Saquon Barkley broke off some big runs and the running game looked good. Barkley ran for 73 yards on 11 carries before halftime and then came out and rushed four times for nine yards in the second half. Jalen Hurts’ pass protection was OK, but some killer penalties and poor execution on 1st and 2nd downs put him behind the sticks most of the night, resulting in an ugly performance in which he threw for just 153 yards with two turnovers. He was shut out in the 2nd half.

He was not helped by his coaching staff. Nick Sirianni’s decision not to go for it on 4th-and-1 near midfield in the 3rd quarter trailing 20-7 reeked of a lack of confidence in his unit. After the game, Sirianni, the team’s CEO head coach who says he specializes in his decision-making in just these kinds of game situations, admitted he made a mistake. He then went for it on 4th-and-5 later in the 4th quarter, after the game had largely been decided. None of it made sense. Play-caller Sean Mannion continues to call screen passes behind the line to Makai Lemon, and receivers weren’t schemed open this week.

It had been a bumpy first two weeks for the Eagles, but they had persevered and managed to pull out two victories against lesser opponents/coaching staffs. Against Ben Johnson’s Bears, they did not receive similar fortune.

Things won’t get any easier when Matthew Stafford comes to Philadelphia this week, looking to exact revenge in his own personal house of horrors. The Rams, 1-2 to start the season, will be out for blood. Then it’s on to Jacksonville to face a Jaguars team that has given up the fewest points in the league through the first three weeks.

If they play like they did last night in Chicago, the Eagles will be staring at a 2-3 record two weeks from now.

item.title: Fantasy football waiver wire: 12 players to add for NFL Week 4
item.description: The biggest injury losses this past week were at the running back position, but there are several potential pickups to fill the void.
item.content:encoded:
Last week, it was the quarterbacks. This week, it's the running backs.

Injuries continue to flummox fantasy football managers as several more key players were sidelined in Week 3. The only remedy is to find the next man up who can fill those empty lineup spots going forward.

One more thing to keep in mind this week: Byes begin in Week 5, so if your fantasy team needs multiple holes filled when the Carolina Panthers and Kansas City Chiefs take their week off, it might be a good idea to be proactive and pick up replacements sooner rather than later.

Fantasy football players to add for Week 4

Due to the wide variance in types of leagues and individual team needs, the players listed here include their availability rates in Yahoo leagues, which may or may not match rates on other platforms. (Suggested bid values based on $100 free agent acquisition budget for the season.)

For customized waiver wire suggestions, synced to your league, subscribe to USA TODAY Sports Fantasy's exclusive tools.

RB Ollie Gordon II, Miami Dolphins (5% rostered)

Gordon is this week's top waiver prize with starting running back De'Von Achane out for the season. His numbers weren't very impressive on Sunday (20 carries, 41 yards) but he did get into the end zone and appears to be the lead back going forward. With a full week of practice under his belt, Gordon should be ready to meet the moment. (Suggested FAAB bid: $32. More if you had Achane)

WR Kalif Raymond, Chicago Bears (10% rostered)

After three games, Raymond − not Luther Burden, Rome Odunze or Colston Loveland − is the Bears' leading receiver. He caught six of his seven targets for 90 yards and a touchdown on Monday night, including a pretty 41-yard catch-and-run. Backup QB Case Keenum was particularly effective, so look for Raymond to continue to be an important part of the offense, even with Caleb Williams sidelined. (FAAB bid: $12)

RB Braelon Allen, New York Jets (20% rostered)

The Jets may have dodged a bullet with Breece Hall's thigh injury not as bad as originally feared. Still, he's considered week-to-week, which leaves plenty of room open for Allen to step forward. The third-year back out of Wisconsin scored a touchdown in Week 2, and he did get seven total touches in Week 3 (four rushes, three receptions). He'll look to solve the Bears defense that shut down the Eagles rushing attack on Monday night. (FAAB bid: $11)

TE Kenyon Sadiq, New York Jets (19% rostered)

The week's big breakout at tight end, Sadiq showed exactly why the Jets made him the 16th overall pick in this year's draft. He caught seven passes on eight targets for 105 yards and a touchdown on Sunday, making his mark with an athletic stretch on the 24-yard TD reception. Don't forget, he also rushed for a TD in the opener. (FAAB bid: $8)

RB Alvin Kamara, New Orleans Saints (43% rostered)

Travis Etienne Jr. exited with a hamstring injury in the third quarter against the Raiders, pushing the 31-year-old Kamara back into the spotlight. He rushed for 36 yards on nine carries and caught his only target while splitting the backfield duties with Kendre Miller. Etienne will miss some time but could be back fairly soon, so there's no need to go after Kamara (or Miller) quite as aggressively. (FAAB bid: $7. Miller, $5 backup)

RB Keaton Mitchell, Los Angeles Chargers (32% rostered)

There are no injury issues in the Chargers backfield, but Mitchell's increased usage in Week 3 does make him an interesting speculative pickup. He went from 17 snaps in each of the first two weeks to 23 on Sunday, while nearly equaling the total (27) for starter Omarion Hampton. Mitchell had a season-high 52 rushing yards on eight carries and also scored on a short TD reception. After battling injuries in his first three NFL seasons, he finally looks healthy. (FAAB bid: $7)

WR Keenan Allen, Indianapolis Colts (22% rostered)

With Alec Pierce on injured reserve with a heel injury, the wily veteran Allen stepped forward against the Texans with six catches for 63 yards and a TD. The Colts don't have a deep receiving corps behind WR Josh Downs and TE Tyler Warren, so if the running game isn't clicking, the 34-year-old Allen should continue to see plenty of targets − as long as he stays healthy. (FAAB bid: $6)

WR Konata Mumpfield, Los Angeles Rams (1% rostered)

Star wideout Puca Nacua missed his second consecutive game with a hip injury, allowing Mumpfield to see eight targets on Sunday night in Denver. He caught four of them for 93 yards and a touchdown, setting career highs across the board. As long as Nacua is out, Mumpfield looks like QB Matthew Stafford's No. 2 target behind Davante Adams. (FAAB bid: $5)

WR Pat Bryant, Denver Broncos (8%)

We're getting into speculative territory now. Bryant has always had the talent, but just hasn't been able to break out. Could Sunday be the starting point? He caught two passes for 44 yards and scored his first TD of the season against the Rams. With Marvin Mims still out, Bryant was on the field for a season-high 47 snaps. (FAAB bid: $3)

WR Chris Bell, Miami Dolphins (4% rostered)

Against Kansas City's top-rated defense against wide receivers, Bell was targeted seven times. The rookie caught four of them for 67 yards in his first extensive action. That was partly due to fellow rookie Caleb Douglas being inactive with an ankle injury. Bell is an imposing physical presence who may just need a chance to show he can produce. (FAAB bid: $3)

RB Ty Johnson, Buffalo Bills (0% rostered)

Johnson missed the first two games of the season with a hamstring injury, but was the clear choice as the Bills' third-down back on Sunday. He caught all four of his targets for 50 yards, while playing only 15 snaps. Look for his usage to increase, making him a borderline add in PPR formats. (FAAB bid: $2)

QB Case Keenum, Chicago Bears (1% rostered)

It's only one game, but the 38-year-old Keenum looked pretty good in his first NFL start since 2024. He completed 24-of-34 passes for 247 yards and two scores, while remaining equisitely calm under pressure. Caleb Williams is likely to miss several more games as his hamstring heals, making Keenum an interesting fill-in as the bye weeks start to roll around. (FYI: The Bears' bye isn't until Week 10.) (FAAB bid: $2)
